title: Colorado Real Estate Broker
description: Prep for the PSI Colorado broker exam: lessons for the national and Colorado state portions, a 458-question bank with timed exams scored like the real thing, notecards, math drills, a glossary and quick-reference sheets. Independent study material, not affiliated with PSI, the Division of Real Estate or any school. Laws and Commission forms change; check current sources.
author: Examiner
changelog: Adds REITs and real-estate securities. Adds Colorado's three principal meridians and a few survey facts. Adds a note on fixture tests: Van Ed's quizzes key method of attachment as most important, while courts treat intention as controlling. Every lesson quiz now has 10 questions: 107 new questions written from the lessons themselves fill the gaps. Earlier in this series: end-of-lesson quizzes (pass with 70% to complete a lesson), a corrected seller-disclosure answer key, and ten new lessons covering federal tax and 1031s, commercial leasing, MLS/IDX and wire fraud, the Colorado closing worksheet, other Commission forms and HOAs, and Commission rules, audits and complaints.

lessons.title: Real vs. personal property, fixtures, and legal descriptions
lessons.body:
## What "real property" means

Everything a broker sells falls into one of two buckets: real property or personal property. The exam tests the line between them constantly, because the line decides what transfers with a deed and what has to be handled with a bill of sale.

- **Land** is the earth's surface, everything below it to the center of the earth, and the airspace above it, plus things permanently attached by nature (trees, minerals in place).
- **Real estate** is land plus everything people permanently attach to it (buildings, fences, paving).
- **[[Real property]]** is real estate plus the legal rights that come with owning it. These rights are often described as the [[bundle of rights]]: possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition.

**[[Personal property]]** (also called *personalty* or *chattels*) is everything movable that isn't real property: furniture, cars, a refrigerator that just plugs in. Personal property transfers by a **bill of sale**, not a deed.

### Rights that can be separated

Ownership can be split into layers, and each layer can be sold or leased separately:

| Right | Covers | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Surface rights | The land's surface | Selling a lot but keeping minerals |
| Subsurface (mineral) rights | Oil, gas, minerals below | An oil company leases mineral rights |
| Air rights | Space above the surface | Selling air rights over a rail yard for a building platform |

Rights and privileges that "run with" the land, such as an easement benefiting the lot or water rights tied to it, are called [[appurtenances]]. They transfer automatically with the property unless the deed says otherwise.

### Water rights in brief

Many eastern states follow **riparian** rights (owners along a river share reasonable use) and **littoral** rights (owners along a lake or ocean). Many western states, including Colorado, use **prior appropriation**: the first person to put water to beneficial use has the senior right, regardless of who owns the riverbank. Colorado water rights are covered in the state portion of this course.

## Crops: emblements vs. natural growth

- **Fructus naturales** (trees, perennial shrubs, grass) grow without yearly planting. They're treated as real property.
- **Fructus industriales** are annual crops planted by human labor (wheat, corn). They're personal property, and they're called [[emblements]]. A tenant farmer who planted a crop generally has the right to come back and harvest it even if the lease ends before harvest, provided the tenant didn't cause the lease to end.

## Fixtures

A **[[fixture]]** is an item that was personal property but has been attached to real property in a way that makes it part of the real estate. A ceiling fan in the box is personal property; once it's wired into the ceiling, it's a fixture and transfers with the house unless the contract excludes it.

Courts use a handful of tests, often remembered as **MARIA**:

- **M**ethod of attachment: is it bolted, nailed, plumbed or wired in? Would removal damage the property?
- **A**daptability: was the item customized for this property (custom-cut blinds, a built-in bookcase)?
- **R**elationship of the parties: courts favor buyers over sellers, and tenants over landlords.
- **I**ntention: did the person who attached it intend it to be permanent? Courts treat intention as the most important test.
- **A**greement: a written agreement between the parties overrides the other tests.

> **Heads-up on "most important":** Courts treat the intention of the person who attached the item as the controlling test, judged objectively from how it was attached and adapted. Some prep courses, including Van Ed's quizzes, instead key **method of attachment** as the most important test. Answer each source on its own terms; on any exam, a written agreement between the parties beats every other test.

> **Exam tip:** The easiest way to prevent a fixture dispute is to address it in the purchase contract. If the seller wants to keep the dining-room chandelier, list it as excluded, or swap it out before showing the home.

### Trade fixtures

A **[[trade fixture]]** is equipment a tenant installs for a business: restaurant ovens, store shelving, a salon's chairs. Trade fixtures stay the tenant's personal property. The tenant must remove them by the end of the lease and repair any damage caused by removal. Trade fixtures left behind after the lease ends may become the landlord's property through **accession**.

## Legal descriptions

A street address isn't precise enough to convey title. A deed needs a **legal description** that identifies exactly one parcel. There are three main methods.

### Metes and bounds

[[Metes and bounds]] is the oldest method. "Metes" are distances and directions; "bounds" are boundaries, often marked by **monuments** (fixed objects such as iron pins, trees, or roads). The description starts at a [[point of beginning]] (POB), runs around the parcel with courses and distances (for example, "north 45 degrees east, 200 feet"), and must **return to the POB**. A description that doesn't close is defective.

If a monument and a measured distance conflict, monuments generally control.

### Lot and block (recorded plat)

When a developer subdivides land, a surveyor prepares a **plat map** showing each lot and block, which is recorded with the county. A deed can then describe a parcel as "Lot 7, Block 3, Aspen Ridge Subdivision, according to the plat recorded in…" This [[lot and block]] method (also called the *recorded plat* system) is the most common description for urban and suburban homes.

### Rectangular (government) survey system

The [[rectangular survey system]], also called the Public Land Survey System, is used across most of the western and midwestern United States, including Colorado. Colorado descriptions are tied to three principal meridians: the **Sixth Principal Meridian** (most of the state), the **New Mexico Principal Meridian** (parts of southwestern and south-central Colorado), and the small **Ute Meridian** near Grand Junction. It's built on a grid:

- **Principal meridians** run north–south; **base lines** run east–west.
- **Range lines** run north–south every 6 miles; **township lines** run east–west every 6 miles.
- The squares they form are **townships**, each 6 miles by 6 miles (36 square miles, or 23,040 acres). A block of 16 townships, 24 miles on a side, is sometimes called a **quadrangle**.
- Each [[township]] is divided into 36 **sections**, numbered 1 through 36 in a back-and-forth (boustrophedon) pattern starting in the northeast corner: section 1 is in the northeast corner, section 6 in the northwest, section 36 in the southeast.
- A [[section]] is 1 mile by 1 mile, which is 1 square mile, or **640 acres**.

Because the earth is curved, the grid can't be perfect. **Correction lines** (every 24 miles) and **government lots** (irregular parcels along water or grid edges) handle the leftovers.

### Acreage math

To find acreage from a rectangular survey description, read the description **backward**, starting at the section, and divide 640 by each fraction's denominator.

Example: *"The NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 of Section 12"*

- Section 12 = 640 acres
- SW 1/4 = 640 ÷ 4 = 160 acres
- NE 1/4 of that = 160 ÷ 4 = **40 acres**

Shortcut: multiply the denominators (4 × 4 = 16) and divide into 640: 640 ÷ 16 = 40.

If the description uses "and" (for example, "the N 1/2 of the NW 1/4 **and** the SE 1/4"), it describes two separate parcels. Compute each one and add them together.

> **Exam tip:** "N 1/2 of the NE 1/4 of the SE 1/4" = 640 ÷ (2 × 4 × 4) = 640 ÷ 32 = 20 acres. The more fractions in the description, the smaller the parcel.

## Land measurement facts to memorize

| Unit | Equals |
|---|---|
| 1 [[acre]] | 43,560 square feet |
| 1 mile | 5,280 feet |
| 1 square mile (section) | 640 acres |
| 1 township | 36 sections = 36 square miles |
| 1 rod | 16.5 feet |
| 1 square yard | 9 square feet |
| 1 acre | 4,840 square yards |

A quick conversion: a rectangular lot 330 feet by 660 feet is 217,800 sq ft ÷ 43,560 = 5 acres.

### Vertical descriptions

Condominium units and air rights need elevation, not just a footprint. Surveyors measure height from a **datum**, a reference point (often mean sea level or a local benchmark). A condo unit's description may refer to the recorded condominium map and declaration.

lessons.title: Estates and forms of ownership
lessons.body:
## Estates in land

An **estate** is the degree, quantity, and duration of an owner's interest in property. Estates fall into two families:

| Freehold estates (ownership) | Leasehold estates (tenancy) |
|---|---|
| Duration is indefinite or measured by a life | Duration is set by a lease |
| Owner holds title | Tenant holds possession; landlord keeps title |
| Fee simple, life estate | Estate for years, periodic, at will, at sufferance |

A [[freehold estate]] is an ownership interest; a [[leasehold estate]] is a tenant's right to possess property owned by someone else. Leaseholds are treated as personal property.

### Fee simple estates

- **[[Fee simple absolute]]** is the most complete ownership the law allows. It has no time limit, it can be sold or left by will, and it passes to heirs if the owner dies without a will. When people say someone "owns" a home, this is usually what they mean.
- **[[Fee simple defeasible]]** is fee ownership that can end if a stated condition happens or stops happening. There are two versions:
  - **Fee simple determinable** uses words of duration like "so long as" or "while." If the condition is broken, title returns to the grantor **automatically**. The grantor's future interest is a **possibility of reverter**.
  - **Fee simple subject to a condition subsequent** uses words like "on condition that" or "provided that." If the condition is broken, the grantor must **take action** to get the property back. The grantor's future interest is a **right of reentry** (power of termination).

> **Exam tip:** "So long as" = automatic reversion (determinable). "On condition that" = grantor must act (condition subsequent).

### Life estates

A **[[life estate]]** lasts for the life of a named person.

- In a **conventional life estate**, the measuring life is the life tenant's own. "To Ann for life."
- In a **life estate pur autre vie**, the measuring life is someone else's. "To Ann for the life of Bob." When Bob dies, Ann's estate ends.

When the life estate ends, the property goes to either:

- the grantor (or the grantor's heirs), which is a **reversion**, or
- a third party named in the deed, the **remainderman**, who holds a **remainder** interest.

The life tenant may live on the property, rent it out, or sell or mortgage the life estate, but can't convey more than they own. A buyer gets only an interest that ends at the measuring death. The life tenant must not commit **waste** (damage that lowers the value for the future owner) and generally pays property taxes and routine upkeep.

**Legal life estates** are created by state law rather than by a deed. Historically these included dower and curtesy (a surviving spouse's interest), and many states have abolished them. **Homestead** laws in many states protect part of the value of a family home from certain creditors.

### Leasehold estates

| Type | Key feature |
|---|---|
| Estate for years | Fixed start and end date (even if shorter than a year); ends without notice |
| Periodic tenancy | Renews automatically each period (month-to-month); ends with proper notice |
| Tenancy at will | No set term; either party can end it; ends on the death of either party |
| Tenancy at sufferance | Tenant holds over without the landlord's consent after the lease ends |

## Forms of ownership

Estates describe *how much* is owned. Forms of ownership describe *who* holds it and how.

### Ownership in severalty

**[[Severalty]]** means one owner, a single person or a single legal entity such as a corporation. The name sounds like "several," which is a classic trap: it means the owner's interest is *severed* from everyone else's.

### Tenancy in common

In a **[[tenancy in common]]** (TIC):

- Each co-owner holds an **undivided interest**: each one may use the whole property and owns no particular square foot of it.
- The shares may be **unequal** (60/40, for example).
- Each owner can sell, mortgage, or leave their share by will **without the others' consent**.
- There is **no right of survivorship**. A deceased owner's share passes to their heirs or devisees.
- Only one unity is required: **possession**.

Any co-owner can ask a court for a **partition** if co-owners can't agree. The court divides the property, or orders it sold and divides the proceeds.

### Joint tenancy

A **[[joint tenancy]]** has one defining feature: the **[[right of survivorship]]**. When a joint tenant dies, the deceased owner's interest passes to the surviving joint tenants automatically. It doesn't go through probate, and a joint tenant can't leave the interest by will.

Creating a joint tenancy traditionally requires the **four unities** (PITT):

- **P**ossession: equal right to possess the whole property
- **I**nterest: equal ownership shares
- **T**ime: interests acquired at the same time
- **T**itle: interests acquired by the same deed or will

If one joint tenant sells their interest, the buyer does **not** become a joint tenant. The buyer holds as a tenant in common with the remaining owners, who stay joint tenants with one another.

> **Exam tip:** A, B, and C are joint tenants. C sells to D. Now A and B are joint tenants with each other, and D is a tenant in common owning 1/3. If A dies, B owns 2/3 and D owns 1/3.

**Colorado note:** Under C.R.S. 38-31-101, when property is conveyed to two or more natural persons, Colorado presumes a tenancy in common unless the deed expressly declares a joint tenancy (for example, "as joint tenants," "in joint tenancy," or "JTWROS"). Only natural persons (and fiduciaries such as co-trustees) can hold as joint tenants in Colorado. Most states have a similar presumption favoring tenancy in common.

### Tenancy by the entirety

**[[Tenancy by the entirety]]** is a special form of co-ownership for married couples, recognized in some states. It works like joint tenancy (survivorship, the four unities plus the unity of marriage), but neither spouse can convey or encumber the property alone, and it's generally protected from creditors of only one spouse. Divorce ends it.

**Colorado note:** Colorado does **not** recognize tenancy by the entirety. C.R.S. 38-31-201 says no conveyance creates one, and a deed that tries to create one creates a joint tenancy instead.

### Community property

In **[[community property]]** states (a minority of states, mostly in the West and Southwest), property acquired during marriage generally belongs to both spouses equally, while property owned before marriage or received by gift or inheritance is **separate property**. Colorado is **not** a community property state. Colorado divides marital property at divorce by equitable distribution.

### Comparison table

| | Severalty | Tenancy in common | Joint tenancy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Number of owners | One | Two or more | Two or more |
| Shares | All | Can be unequal | Equal |
| Survivorship | n/a | No; goes to heirs | Yes; goes to survivors |
| Can owner sell share? | Yes | Yes | Yes, but it breaks the joint tenancy for that share |
| Unities required | n/a | Possession | Possession, interest, time, title |

## Special ownership arrangements

### Condominiums

In a **[[condominium]]**, each owner holds **fee simple title to an individual unit** (generally the airspace inside the walls) plus an **undivided interest, as a tenant in common, in the common elements** (hallways, roof, grounds, pool). Some areas are **limited common elements** reserved for one unit, such as an assigned parking space or a balcony. A recorded **declaration** creates the condominium, and an owners' association manages it, funded by assessments. Unpaid assessments can become a lien on the unit.

### Cooperatives

In a **[[cooperative]]** (co-op), a corporation owns the building. Residents buy **shares of stock** in the corporation and receive a **proprietary lease** for their unit. Because the buyer owns stock rather than real estate, a co-op interest is usually treated as **personal property**. The co-op board often must approve buyers. If other shareholders stop paying their share of building costs, a blanket mortgage default can endanger everyone.

### Timeshares

A **[[timeshare]]** divides use of a property by time:

- A **timeshare estate** conveys a fee interest for a recurring period (for example, week 22 every year).
- A **timeshare use** (right-to-use) is a contractual or lease-type right to use the property for a period, without real property ownership.

### Trusts

In a **[[trust]]**, a **trustor** (also called the settlor or grantor) conveys property to a **trustee**, who holds legal title and manages it for a **beneficiary**. Common types include living (inter vivos) trusts, testamentary trusts (created by a will), and land trusts (where the beneficiary often keeps control and the trust keeps the beneficiary's identity private).

### Business ownership

- **Corporation:** a separate legal entity that holds title in severalty. Shareholders have limited liability, but a C corporation's income is taxed at the corporate level and again as dividends ("double taxation").
- **General partnership:** all partners share management and unlimited liability.
- **Limited partnership:** at least one general partner manages and has unlimited liability; limited partners are passive investors whose liability is limited to their investment.
- **Limited liability company (LLC):** members get limited liability with flexible, pass-through tax treatment. LLCs are popular for holding investment property.
- **Syndicate / joint venture:** a group pooling money for one investment or project. These are arrangements, not separate legal forms, and are often organized as partnerships or LLCs.
- **Real estate investment trust (REIT):** a company that pools investors' money to own or finance real estate and, if it meets federal tax rules, passes income through without paying corporate income tax. The key tests: at least **100 owners**, no more than half owned by five or fewer individuals, at least **75% of gross income** from real-estate sources such as rents and mortgage interest, and at least **90% of taxable income** paid out to owners each year. (Older textbooks say 95%; the requirement dropped to 90% in 2001.)

> **Exam tip:** When a buyer gives up management control for a passive return, such as a condo unit that must go into a mandatory rental pool, the deal can be a **security**. Selling securities takes a securities license and registration, not just a real estate license.

lessons.title: Encumbrances: liens, easements, encroachments, and adverse possession
lessons.body:
## What an encumbrance is

An **[[encumbrance]]** is any claim, right, or interest held by someone other than the owner that lowers the property's value or limits its use. Encumbrances don't necessarily stop a sale, but the buyer takes the property subject to them unless they're cleared.

There are two broad groups:

- **Money claims:** liens.
- **Physical or use limits:** easements, encroachments, deed restrictions.

## Liens

A **[[lien]]** is a creditor's claim against property as security for a debt. If the debt isn't paid, the creditor can force a sale of the property (foreclose) to collect.

### Classifying liens

| Classification | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Voluntary | Owner chooses to create it | Mortgage, deed of trust |
| Involuntary | Created by law without the owner's consent | Tax lien, judgment lien, mechanic's lien |
| Specific | Attaches to one particular property | Mortgage, property tax, special assessment, mechanic's lien |
| General | Attaches to all of a debtor's property in the area | Judgment lien, federal income tax lien, estate/inheritance tax lien |

A mortgage, then, is **voluntary and specific**. A judgment lien is **involuntary and general**.

### Common liens

- **Mortgage / deed of trust lien:** secures a loan used to buy or refinance the property.
- **Property tax lien:** created by law for unpaid ad valorem taxes.
- **Special assessment lien:** for public improvements that benefit specific properties.
- **[[Mechanic's lien]]:** protects contractors, subcontractors, and suppliers who improved the property and weren't paid. In many states its priority can date back to when work began or materials were first delivered, not to when the lien was filed. That's why title insurers worry about recent construction.
- **Judgment lien:** a court judgment against a person becomes a general lien on that person's real property in the county where it's recorded.
- **Federal tax liens:** for unpaid federal income or estate taxes.

### Lien priority

The basic rule is **first in time, first in right**: liens rank by the date and time they were recorded. The big exception is that **property tax and special assessment liens generally take priority over all other liens**, no matter when they were recorded.

A lender with an earlier lien can agree to move behind a later lien by signing a **[[subordination]] agreement**. This often happens when a landowner's existing loan is subordinated to a construction loan.

> **Exam tip:** A seller has a 2019 mortgage, a 2023 judgment lien, and unpaid property taxes for this year. On a foreclosure sale, the property taxes get paid first, then the mortgage, then the judgment.

## Easements

An **[[easement]]** is a right to use another person's land for a specific purpose, such as a driveway, utility line, or path to a lake. An easement is a non-possessory interest in land: the holder may use the land but doesn't own it or possess it.

### Easement appurtenant

An **[[easement appurtenant]]** involves two parcels:

- The **dominant tenement** (dominant estate) is the parcel that *benefits* from the easement.
- The **servient tenement** (servient estate) is the parcel that *carries the burden*, the land that is crossed.

An easement appurtenant **runs with the land**. If either parcel is sold, the easement continues: the new owner of the dominant parcel keeps the right, and the new owner of the servient parcel takes subject to it.

### Easement in gross

An **[[easement in gross]]** has a servient tenement but **no dominant tenement**. It benefits a person or company rather than a neighboring parcel.

- **Commercial** easements in gross (utility lines, pipelines, railroad rights-of-way) are usually transferable.
- **Personal** easements in gross (a right for one individual to fish on a pond, for example) usually end when that person dies or sells.

### How easements are created

- **Express grant or reservation:** written in a deed or separate agreement.
- **Easement by necessity:** created by law when a parcel is sold with no access to a road (landlocked) and the parcels were once under common ownership.
- **Easement by implication:** implied from the circumstances and prior use when land is divided.
- **[[Prescriptive easement]]:** acquired by using someone else's land openly, continuously, and without permission for the period set by state law. It's similar to adverse possession, but it gains a *right to use*, not ownership.
- **Condemnation:** a government or utility acquires an easement through eminent domain.
- **Party wall:** a shared wall on a property line, with each owner holding an easement in the half owned by the other.

### How easements end

- **Merger:** one person comes to own both the dominant and servient parcels.
- **Release:** the dominant owner releases it in writing (often by quitclaim deed).
- **Abandonment:** the holder intentionally gives it up, shown by conduct, not just non-use.
- **Purpose ends:** an easement by necessity ends when another access road is built.
- **Non-use** of a prescriptive easement for the statutory period, in some states.

## Licenses

A **[[license]]** is **personal, revocable permission** to enter someone's land for a specific purpose, such as a ticket to a concert, permission to hunt, or a neighbor letting you park in a driveway. A license is **not** an interest in land, it doesn't run with the land, and it can generally be revoked at any time. It ends when either party dies or the land is sold.

> **Exam tip:** Easement = interest in land, usually in writing, not easily revoked. License = personal privilege, revocable, no interest in land.

## Encroachments

An **[[encroachment]]** happens when an improvement on one property extends onto a neighbor's land or into a setback or easement area. Examples include a fence 3 feet over the line, a garage built partly on the next lot, or roof eaves hanging over the boundary.

- Encroachments are usually discovered by a **survey**. A standard title insurance policy generally doesn't cover them (see the transfer-of-title lesson).
- Left alone long enough, an encroachment can lead to a claim of adverse possession or a prescriptive easement.
- The neighbor's remedies include a lawsuit for removal (an injunction) or damages.

## Adverse possession

**[[Adverse possession]]** is a way to gain **title** to someone else's land by occupying it for the period set by state law. It is a form of **involuntary alienation** for the record owner.

The possession must generally be:

- **O**pen and
- **N**otorious (visible, so the true owner could discover it)
- **C**ontinuous for the statutory period
- **E**xclusive (not shared with the owner or the public)
- **A**dverse, also called hostile (without the owner's permission)

Many students remember these as **OCEAN** or **ONCEA**. Permission defeats a claim: a tenant or someone with a license can't adversely possess, because their use isn't hostile.

**Tacking:** in many states, successive adverse possessors who are in **privity** (for example, a buyer who takes over from a seller) can add their periods together to reach the statutory time.

To get marketable record title, the adverse possessor usually files a **[[quiet title action]]**.

**Colorado note:** Under C.R.S. 38-41-101, the period in Colorado is **18 years**. For fee-title claims filed on or after July 1, 2008, the claimant must prove each element by **clear and convincing evidence** and must show that the claimant (or a predecessor) had a **reasonable, good-faith belief** that they were the actual owner. The court may also order the successful claimant to compensate the former owner. Adverse possession doesn't run against state or local government land. Statutory periods vary widely among states, so the national exam usually asks about elements rather than a specific number of years.

## Deed restrictions as encumbrances

Private restrictions recorded in a deed or a subdivision declaration are also encumbrances. They limit what an owner may build or do. These are covered with land use controls in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Land use controls: public and private
lessons.body:
## Public and private controls

An owner's rights aren't unlimited. Land use is shaped by:

- **Public controls:** government powers over private property.
- **Private controls:** restrictions created by owners and developers through deeds and recorded declarations.

## The four government powers (PETE)

Government's rights over private land are summarized as **PETE**:

| Power | What it does | Compensation? |
|---|---|---|
| **P**olice power | Regulates use for public health, safety, morals, and welfare | No |
| **E**minent domain | Takes private property for public use | Yes, just compensation |
| **T**axation | Levies taxes and special assessments, enforced by liens | n/a |
| **E**scheat | Takes property when an owner dies with no will and no heirs | No |

### Police power

**[[Police power]]** is the government's authority to regulate property use to protect the public. It's the source of zoning, building codes, subdivision rules, environmental regulations, and rent controls. Regulation under the police power doesn't require compensation, as long as it doesn't go so far that it effectively takes the property.

### Eminent domain

**[[Eminent domain]]** is the government's power to take private property for **public use** with **just compensation** (usually fair market value). **Condemnation** is the legal process used to exercise it. Governments and certain entities with delegated authority (utilities, for example) can use it to build roads, schools, pipelines, or power lines.

- The owner can challenge whether the use is public or whether the payment is fair, but generally can't stop a valid taking.
- **[[Inverse condemnation]]** is a lawsuit an *owner* brings when government action has effectively taken or damaged the property (for example, an airport's flight path) without a formal condemnation.
- A partial taking may include **severance damages** for the drop in value of the remaining land.

### Taxation

Local governments levy **ad valorem** (by value) property taxes, which become a specific lien on the property. A **[[special assessment]]** is a charge against only the properties that benefit from a specific public improvement, such as new sidewalks, sewer lines, or street paving. Special assessments are specific, involuntary liens, and like property taxes they generally have priority over other liens.

### Escheat

**[[Escheat]]** transfers property to the state (or county) when an owner dies **without a will and without heirs**. It also applies to some abandoned property. Escheat keeps property from becoming ownerless.

## Planning and zoning

Cities and counties usually adopt a **comprehensive plan** (master plan) for future growth. They then carry it out through **[[zoning]]** ordinances, which divide land into districts and set the allowed uses in each. States give local governments this authority through **enabling acts**.

Zoning ordinances commonly regulate:

- **Use:** residential, commercial, industrial, agricultural, mixed-use, planned unit development (PUD).
- **Density:** units per acre, minimum lot size.
- **Bulk and placement:** building height, lot coverage, **setbacks** from lot lines, floor-area ratio.
- **Aesthetics:** historic districts, signage.

Related concepts:

- **Buffer zone:** a strip (such as a park or a light-use district) separating incompatible uses, like homes and heavy industry.
- **Cumulative zoning** allows "higher" uses in a "lower" zone (a home in a commercial zone). **Exclusive zoning** allows only the listed use.
- **Downzoning:** rezoning to a less intense use (commercial to residential, for example).
- **Spot zoning:** rezoning a single parcel in a way that benefits one owner and conflicts with the comprehensive plan. It is often struck down as illegal.
- **Rezoning (amendment):** changing the zoning of an area through the legislative process.

### Exceptions to zoning

These three show up on almost every exam:

**[[Nonconforming use]]:** a use that was legal when it started but doesn't fit a newer zoning ordinance. It is usually allowed to continue ("grandfathered"). Common limits: the owner usually can't expand it, and if the structure is destroyed or the use is abandoned for a certain time, the right to continue may be lost.

**[[Variance]]:** permission to depart from the *strict requirements* of the ordinance, usually physical standards such as setbacks, height, or lot coverage, because applying them would cause an **unusual hardship** tied to the property (an odd lot shape or steep slope, for example). The hardship can't be self-created, and a variance generally can't be used to bring in a use the zone doesn't allow.

**[[Conditional use permit]]** (also called a *special use permit* or *special exception*): permission for a use the ordinance **lists as allowed if conditions are met**, because it serves the community. Examples include a church, school, or hospital in a residential zone. The approval comes with conditions (parking, hours, landscaping).

| Tool | Why it's granted | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Nonconforming use | Use existed before the rule | Corner store in an area later zoned residential |
| Variance | Hardship from strict rules | Reduced setback on an irregular lot |
| Conditional use | Ordinance allows it with conditions | Church in a residential zone |

> **Exam tip:** "Existed first" = nonconforming use. "Hardship" = variance. "Public benefit, with conditions" = conditional use.

Zoning decisions are typically made by a planning commission and a **board of adjustment** (zoning board of appeals), which hears variance requests and appeals.

## Building codes

**[[Building codes]]** set minimum construction standards for structure, plumbing, electrical, fire safety, and energy use. They're enforced through **building permits** and inspections. When the work passes final inspection, the building department issues a **certificate of occupancy**, which allows people to legally occupy the building. When a zoning rule and a building code (or any two rules) conflict, the **stricter** standard generally controls.

## Subdivision regulations

When a developer divides raw land into lots, local subdivision regulations control street layout and width, utilities, drainage, lot size, open space, and dedication of land for public use. The developer submits a **plat** for approval and records it, which creates the lot-and-block legal descriptions. Developers may also have to pay **impact fees** to fund the schools, parks, and roads new growth requires.

At the federal level, the **Interstate Land Sales Full Disclosure Act** requires developers who sell or lease certain unimproved lots through interstate commerce to register with the federal government and give buyers a **property report** before they sign, unless an exemption applies.

## Environmental regulation (brief)

Federal and state laws address hazards such as lead-based paint, asbestos, radon, underground storage tanks, and contaminated land. Under the federal Superfund law (CERCLA), current and past owners can be liable for cleanup costs, which is why commercial buyers order environmental site assessments. Disclosure duties are covered in other modules.

## Private controls

### Deed restrictions and covenants

A **[[deed restriction]]** limits how a buyer may use the property. A grantor writes it into a deed, or a developer records it for a whole subdivision. Restrictions can be:

- **Covenants:** promises. If one is broken, the remedy is usually a court order (an **injunction**) or damages.
- **Conditions:** if broken, the grantor may be able to reclaim title (see fee simple defeasible). Courts dislike forfeiture, so they interpret restrictions as covenants when they can.

Restrictions that discriminate based on race or other protected classes are **unenforceable** under fair housing law and court decisions, even if they're still in old recorded documents.

### CC&Rs and HOAs

In most planned communities and condominiums, the developer records a declaration of **[[CC&Rs]]** (covenants, conditions, and restrictions) that binds every lot. CC&Rs typically cover architectural approval, fences, paint colors, pets, parking, rentals, and maintenance. They **run with the land** and bind later buyers who take with constructive notice from the recorded declaration.

A **[[homeowners' association]]** (HOA) enforces the CC&Rs, maintains common areas, and charges **assessments** (regular dues and special assessments). Unpaid assessments can become a lien on the owner's property.

A neighbor or the HOA can enforce restrictions by seeking an **injunction**. If they wait too long, the court may refuse to enforce the restriction under the doctrine of **laches** (unreasonable delay). Restrictions may also end by their own terms, by agreement of the owners, or when conditions in the neighborhood change enough that the restriction no longer makes sense.

> **Exam tip:** When a private restriction and a public law both apply, the **more restrictive** one generally governs. A zoning ordinance allowing 35-foot buildings doesn't override CC&Rs limiting homes to one story.

Colorado has its own common-interest community statute (CCIOA) with HOA rules. Those are covered in the state portion of this course.

lessons.title: Transfer of title: deeds, title insurance, recording, and foreclosure
lessons.body:
## How title changes hands

**Title** is ownership, and the evidence of ownership. **Alienation** is any transfer of title.

| Voluntary alienation | Involuntary alienation |
|---|---|
| Sale or gift by **deed** | **Descent** under intestacy laws |
| Transfer by **will** (devise) | **Escheat** to the state |
| | **Eminent domain** |
| | **Foreclosure** and tax sales |
| | **Adverse possession** |
| | Natural forces: **accretion** (land added slowly by water deposits), **erosion**, avulsion |

**[[Involuntary alienation]]** is a transfer of title without the owner's consent.

## Deeds

A **[[deed]]** is the written document that conveys title to real property from the **[[grantor]]** (the person giving title) to the **[[grantee]]** (the person receiving it).

### Requirements for a valid deed

- **In writing**, as the statute of frauds requires
- A **competent grantor** (legal age and sound mind)
- A **grantee** who can be identified (the grantee doesn't need to be competent; a minor can receive title)
- A recital of **consideration** ("for ten dollars and other good and valuable consideration"). A gift deed is valid too.
- A **granting clause** with words of conveyance ("grants," "conveys")
- An adequate **legal description**
- The **grantor's signature** (the grantee usually doesn't sign)
- **Delivery and acceptance**: title passes when the deed is delivered to and accepted by the grantee during the grantor's lifetime

Some deeds also include a **habendum clause** ("to have and to hold"), which defines the estate granted, and exceptions and reservations (for example, reserving mineral rights).

**[[Acknowledgment]]** is a formal declaration before a notary or other authorized officer that the signature is genuine and voluntary. In most states it isn't needed for a deed to be *valid* between the parties, but it's required to **record** the deed. (Colorado's statute, C.R.S. 38-35-106, is more forgiving: a recorded instrument gives notice even if the acknowledgment is missing or defective. In practice, Colorado deeds are still notarized.)

> **Exam tip:** Title passes on **delivery and acceptance**, not when the deed is signed and not when it's recorded. A deed found in a desk drawer after the grantor's death was never delivered and doesn't convey title.

### Types of deeds

| Deed | Warranties given | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **[[General warranty deed]]** | The most protection. Grantor warrants title against defects **at any time**, including before the grantor owned it | Standard sale where the buyer wants full protection |
| **[[Special warranty deed]]** | Grantor warrants only against defects arising **while the grantor owned** the property | Corporate sellers, lenders selling REO property, some fiduciaries |
| **[[Bargain and sale deed]]** | Implies the grantor holds title; gives no express warranties against encumbrances (in some states with limited covenants) | Tax sales, some foreclosures |
| **[[Quitclaim deed]]** | **No warranties.** Conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any | Clearing a cloud on title, releasing an interest, transfers between family members or after divorce |
| **[[Personal representative's deed]]** | Fiduciary deed from an estate | Selling a deceased person's property through probate |

The usual covenants in a general warranty deed are:

- **Seisin:** the grantor owns the property and has the right to convey it.
- **Against encumbrances:** there are no encumbrances except those listed.
- **Quiet enjoyment:** no one with a better title will disturb the grantee's possession.
- **Further assurance:** the grantor will sign any papers needed to perfect the title.
- **Warranty forever:** the grantor will defend the title against lawful claims.

Other fiduciary and court deeds include the **trustee's deed** (from a trustee), **sheriff's deed** (after a court-ordered sale), and **guardian's** or **conservator's deeds**. Fiduciary deeds generally carry only limited warranties. Colorado's Commission-approved deed forms include warranty, special warranty, bargain and sale, and quitclaim deeds.

> **Exam tip:** A quitclaim deed conveys the grantor's interest, if any. It does **not** promise the grantor owns anything. That's what makes it the go-to tool for removing a [[cloud on title]].

## Recording and notice

**[[Recording]]** means filing a deed, mortgage, lien, or other document with the county recorder (the county clerk and recorder in Colorado). Recording isn't required for a deed to be valid between grantor and grantee, but it protects the grantee against later claimants.

- **[[Constructive notice]]:** what the law presumes everyone knows, because it's in the public records or could be found by inspecting the property. A buyer is charged with knowing about recorded documents and about the rights of anyone in possession.
- **[[Actual notice]]:** what a person really knows, whether because they saw it, were told it, or read it.

States use different recording statutes to settle conflicts between two buyers of the same property:

- **Race:** the first to record wins.
- **Notice:** a later buyer without notice of the earlier deed wins.
- **Race-notice:** a later buyer wins only if they had no notice **and** recorded first.

**Colorado note:** C.R.S. 38-35-109 describes Colorado's statute as a race-notice recording statute.

## Evidence of title

- **[[Chain of title]]:** the sequence of recorded conveyances from the original source of title to the current owner. A missing link is a **gap** in the chain.
- **[[Abstract of title]]:** a condensed history of all recorded documents affecting the property. It's not insurance; an attorney reads it and gives an **attorney's opinion of title**.
- **[[Title insurance]]:** a policy that pays for covered losses from title defects. The insurer issues a **title commitment** before closing, listing requirements to be met and exceptions the policy won't cover.

**[[Marketable title]]** is title free enough from reasonable doubt that a prudent buyer would accept it. It doesn't have to be perfect, but it shouldn't expose the buyer to likely lawsuits. Purchase contracts usually require the seller to deliver marketable title. A **cloud on title** (an old unreleased mortgage, a possible heir's claim) can be removed by a quitclaim deed from the claimant or by a **[[quiet title action]]**.

### Owner's vs. lender's title policies

| | Owner's policy | Lender's (loan) policy |
|---|---|---|
| Protects | The buyer/owner | The lender |
| Amount | Usually the purchase price | Usually the loan amount; coverage drops as the loan is paid down |
| Duration | As long as the insured or their heirs hold an interest | Until the loan is paid off |
| Premium | One-time, paid at closing | One-time, paid at closing |

### Standard vs. extended coverage

- **Standard coverage** protects against defects in the public records plus certain hidden risks such as forgery, a grantor's incompetence, improper delivery, and undisclosed heirs. It usually **excludes** matters that only an inspection or survey would reveal: **rights of parties in possession**, boundary disputes and **encroachments**, **unrecorded easements**, and **unrecorded mechanic's liens**.
- **Extended coverage** removes some or all of those standard exceptions, usually after a survey and inspection.

No policy covers defects the insured created or already knew about, or government regulations like zoning.

## Closing basics

At **closing** (settlement), the buyer pays the purchase price, the seller delivers the deed, liens are paid off, the new loan is funded, and documents are recorded. Closing is commonly handled by a **settlement agent**, such as a title company, escrow agent, or attorney. A **closing statement** accounts for every debit and credit, including **prorations** of taxes, rents, and HOA dues. Colorado closing practice is covered in the state portion of this course.

## Foreclosure and alternatives

A **[[foreclosure]]** is the legal process a lender uses to sell a property to satisfy a defaulted loan.

- **Judicial foreclosure:** the lender sues, and a court orders a sale (often conducted by a sheriff).
- **Nonjudicial foreclosure:** a **power of sale** in the deed of trust allows a trustee to sell without a lawsuit. Colorado uses a **public trustee** system for most deed-of-trust foreclosures (details in the state module).
- **Equity of redemption:** the borrower's right to pay off the debt and stop the foreclosure *before* the sale.
- **Statutory redemption:** a right some states give to buy the property back *after* the sale for a set period.
- **Deficiency judgment:** if the sale brings less than the debt, the lender may be able to get a personal judgment for the shortfall, where state law allows.

Alternatives:

- **[[Deed in lieu of foreclosure]]:** the borrower voluntarily deeds the property to the lender. The lender takes title subject to junior liens, so lenders often refuse it when other liens exist.
- **[[Short sale]]:** the property sells for less than the loan balance, and the **lender agrees** to accept the net proceeds as payment. Lender approval is essential, and the lender may or may not release the borrower from the remaining balance.

## Wills, probate, and intestacy

- A **will** lets a person (the **testator**) direct how property passes at death. Real property left by will is a **devise**, and the recipient is a **devisee**. A **codicil** amends a will.
- **Probate** is the court-supervised process of proving a will, paying debts, and distributing property. The court appoints a **personal representative** (also called an executor if named in the will, or an administrator if there's no will) who can sell estate property with a personal representative's deed.
- A person who dies without a valid will dies **[[intestate]]**. State **intestate succession** (descent) statutes decide which relatives inherit. If there are no heirs, the property **escheats** to the state.
- Property held in **joint tenancy** passes to the surviving joint tenants outside probate, and property in a trust passes under the trust terms.

> **Exam tip:** "Testate" means with a will (property passes by devise). "Intestate" means without a will (property passes by descent). No will and no heirs means escheat.

lessons.title: Appraisal and valuation
lessons.body:
## Value, price and cost are three different things

The exam loves to test whether you can keep these apart:

| Term | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Value** | What the property is worth to typical buyers (an estimate) | An appraiser concludes $410,000 |
| **Price** | What a buyer actually paid | The contract closed at $425,000 |
| **Cost** | What it took (or would take) to build | Land plus construction = $380,000 |

[[Market value]] is the most probable price a property should bring in a competitive, open market when buyer and seller are typically motivated, well informed, acting in their own interests, given reasonable exposure time, and paid in cash or its equivalent. An appraisal estimates *value*. [[Market price]] is what was actually paid, and it can differ from value when one party is under pressure, related, or uninformed.

## The four elements of value (DUST)

For a property to have value it needs all four:

- **D**emand — buyers who want it *and* have the purchasing power to buy it
- **U**tility — it can be used for something useful
- **S**carcity — the supply is limited relative to demand
- **T**ransferability — ownership can legally pass to someone else

> **Exam tip:** "Demand" on the exam means *effective* demand — desire backed by the ability to pay.

## Principles of value

- **[[Substitution]]** — a buyer won't pay more for a property than the cost of acquiring an equally desirable substitute. This is the foundation of all three approaches, and especially of the sales comparison approach.
- **[[Highest and best use]]** — the use that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible and maximally productive. An appraiser looks at the land as if vacant and as improved.
- **Conformity** — value is maximized when a property is reasonably similar to its neighbors in style, age and use.
- **[[Contribution]]** — a component is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost. A $60,000 pool that adds $20,000 of value contributes $20,000.
- **Progression and [[Regression]]** — a modest home among nicer homes gains value (progression); the best home on a modest street loses value (regression). Overbuilding for the neighborhood is a regression problem.
- **Anticipation** — value is the present worth of expected future benefits. This principle drives the income approach.
- **Supply and demand** — more supply relative to demand pushes prices down; less pushes them up.
- **Change** — nothing stays the same. Neighborhoods move through growth, stability, decline and sometimes revitalization.

## Who may give an opinion of value?

An [[Appraisal]] is a formal, unbiased opinion of value prepared by an appraiser who holds a state credential. Federally related transactions above certain thresholds must use a state-licensed or state-certified appraiser, and most mortgage lenders require an appraisal for a purchase loan. Credential levels typically run from licensed to certified residential to certified general, with higher levels covering larger or more complex properties. In Colorado, appraisers are credentialed through the Division of Real Estate, separately from broker licensing.

A broker usually prepares a [[Comparative market analysis]] (CMA) to help a seller set a list price or a buyer decide on an offer. A [[Broker price opinion]] (BPO) is a similar estimate, often ordered by a lender or asset manager. Neither is an appraisal, and a broker should never call one an appraisal or represent it as one. Unless you also hold an appraiser credential, stay in the lane of market analysis.

> **Exam tip:** If a question asks what a broker produces to help set a listing price, the answer is a CMA, not an appraisal.

## The three approaches to value

An appraiser usually considers all three, then **reconciles** them into one final opinion by weighting the approach most suited to the property type. Reconciliation is not a simple average.

### 1. Sales comparison (market data) approach

Best for single-family homes and vacant land. The appraiser picks recent sales of similar properties ([[Comparables]]) and adjusts each **comparable** toward the subject.

The golden rule: **adjust the comp, never the subject.**
- Comp is *better* than the subject → subtract (CBS: Comp Better, Subtract).
- Comp is *worse* → add (CIA: Comp Inferior, Add).

**Worked example.** A comp sold for $400,000. It has a garage worth $15,000 that the subject lacks, and the subject has an extra bathroom worth $10,000.
1. Comp has the garage (comp better) → $400,000 − $15,000 = $385,000
2. Subject has the extra bath (comp worse) → $385,000 + $10,000 = $395,000
3. Adjusted value indicated by this comp: **$395,000**

### 2. Cost approach

Best for new construction and special-purpose properties with few sales (schools, churches, fire stations).

**Value = Land value + (Replacement or reproduction cost new − Accrued depreciation)**

- **Reproduction cost** — an exact replica with the same materials.
- **Replacement cost** — a building with the same utility using modern materials. More common.

**Worked example.** A 2,000 sq ft building costs $180/sq ft to replace. Accrued depreciation is $70,000 and the land is worth $90,000.
1. Cost new: 2,000 × $180 = $360,000
2. Less depreciation: $360,000 − $70,000 = $290,000
3. Add land: $290,000 + $90,000 = **$380,000**

### Depreciation types

[[Depreciation]] in appraisal is any loss in value from any cause.

| Type | Cause | Curable? |
|---|---|---|
| **Physical deterioration** | Wear and tear: worn roof, peeling paint | Curable or incurable |
| **[[Functional obsolescence]]** | Poor design or outdated features: one bath in a 5-bedroom house, odd floor plan | Curable or incurable |
| **[[External obsolescence]]** (economic) | Something *off* the property: new highway noise, a closing factory, rezoning nearby | Always **incurable** |

"Curable" means the cost to fix it is no more than the value it adds; "incurable" means it is not economically sensible (or not possible) to fix.

> **Exam tip:** External obsolescence is always incurable because the owner can't fix something outside the property line. Land does not depreciate — only improvements do.

### 3. Income approach

Best for income-producing property (apartments, offices, retail). It applies the principle of anticipation. Steps:

1. Potential gross income (all units, full occupancy)
2. Minus vacancy and collection loss → effective gross income
3. Minus operating expenses → **[[Net operating income]]** (NOI)
4. Value = NOI ÷ [[Capitalization rate]]

Operating expenses include taxes, insurance, maintenance, management and utilities. They do **not** include mortgage payments (debt service) or the owner's income tax depreciation.

**Worked example.** A fourplex: potential gross income $96,000, vacancy 5%, operating expenses $40,000, cap rate 8%.
1. Vacancy: $96,000 × 0.05 = $4,800 → EGI $91,200
2. NOI: $91,200 − $40,000 = $51,200
3. Value: $51,200 ÷ 0.08 = **$640,000**

A higher cap rate means a lower value for the same NOI (more risk, lower price).

### Gross rent and gross income multipliers

A quick income tool for small rentals:
- **[[Gross rent multiplier]] (GRM)** = Sales price ÷ *monthly* gross rent. Used for 1–4 unit homes.
- **[[Gross income multiplier]] (GIM)** = Sales price ÷ *annual* gross income. Used for larger or commercial property.

**Worked example.** Comparable rentals sold for about 150 times monthly rent. The subject rents for $2,200/month.
Value ≈ $2,200 × 150 = **$330,000**.

## Automated valuation models

An [[Automated valuation model]] (AVM) uses software and public-record and sales data to estimate value without an inspection. Online "home value estimates" are AVMs. They are fast and cheap but can't see condition, upgrades or view, so they're least reliable in neighborhoods with few similar sales.

lessons.title: Financing concepts: notes, liens and clauses
lessons.body:
## Two documents: the debt and the security

Almost every real estate loan has two instruments:

- **[[Promissory note]]** — the borrower's personal promise to repay. It states the amount, rate, payment terms and what happens on default. The note *is* the debt.
- **Security instrument** — a [[Mortgage]] or a [[Deed of trust]] that pledges the real property as collateral for the note. It creates a lien.

| | Mortgage | Deed of trust |
|---|---|---|
| Parties | Two: mortgagor (borrower) and mortgagee (lender) | Three: trustor (borrower), beneficiary (lender), trustee |
| Typical foreclosure | Judicial in many states | Non-judicial power of sale in many states |
| On payoff | Satisfaction of mortgage | Release (reconveyance) |

Colorado home loans are secured almost entirely by deeds of trust, and the trustee is ordinarily the county [[Public trustee]], who handles releases and foreclosures.

> **Exam tip:** The *borrower* gives the mortgage; the lender receives it. "Mortgagor" = borrower. If the exam says the mortgagor signed, it means the borrower.

### Lien theory vs title theory

- **[[Lien theory]]** — the borrower holds title; the lender just holds a lien. Most states.
- **Title theory** — legal title is conveyed to the lender (or a trustee) until the loan is paid; the borrower keeps equitable title and possession.
- Some states are a hybrid ("intermediate theory").

## Clauses you must know

- **[[Acceleration clause]]** — on default, the lender can declare the *entire* balance due immediately. Foreclosure usually follows if the borrower can't pay.
- **[[Alienation clause]]** (due-on-sale) — if the borrower transfers the property, the lender can call the loan due. It prevents an unapproved assumption.
- **Prepayment penalty clause** — charges a fee for paying off early. Without one, the borrower may generally prepay.
- **[[Defeasance clause]]** — requires the lender to release the lien once the debt is paid in full.
- **[[Subordination]] clause** — the lender agrees its lien will rank behind a later lien (common with land loans that will be followed by a construction loan).
- **[[Release clause]]** — in a blanket loan covering several lots, lets individual parcels be released as they are sold and a set amount is paid down.

### Assumption vs "subject to"

- **Assumption** — the buyer takes over the loan and becomes personally liable. The seller stays secondarily liable unless the lender grants a **novation** (release of liability).
- **Subject to** — the buyer takes title and makes payments but is *not* personally liable; the seller remains liable.

## Points, LTV and mortgage insurance

**[[Discount points]].** One point = 1% of the **loan amount** (not the price). Discount points are prepaid interest that buy down the rate. An origination fee may also be quoted in points.

**[[Loan-to-value ratio]] (LTV)** = loan amount ÷ the *lesser* of price or appraised value. A $360,000 loan on a home appraised at $400,000 and bought for $410,000 has an LTV of $360,000 ÷ $400,000 = 90%.

**[[Private mortgage insurance]] (PMI)** protects the *lender* on a conventional loan when the borrower's down payment is small (classically when LTV is above 80%). It is not life insurance and does not protect the borrower. Federal law provides ways to cancel it as equity builds; on government-insured loans the comparable cost is called a mortgage insurance premium.

**[[PITI]]** = Principal, Interest, Taxes, Insurance — the full monthly housing payment when the lender collects taxes and insurance into an **escrow (impound) account**.

## Underwriting

[[Underwriting]] is the lender's evaluation of whether to make the loan. Think of the "four Cs":

1. **Capacity** — can the borrower afford the payment? Lenders look at income stability and two ratios:
   - **Housing (front-end) ratio** = housing payment (PITI plus things like HOA dues) ÷ gross monthly income
   - **Total debt (back-end) ratio** = housing payment + other monthly debts ÷ gross monthly income
2. **Credit** — history of paying debts, reflected in credit reports and scores.
3. **Capital** — cash for the down payment, closing costs and reserves.
4. **Collateral** — the property, supported by the appraisal.

Specific ratio caps and score minimums vary by loan program and change over time, so the exam focuses on what the ratios measure, not today's limits.

**Worked example.** Gross monthly income $8,000, PITI $2,000, car and card payments $800.
- Housing ratio: $2,000 ÷ $8,000 = 25%
- Total debt ratio: ($2,000 + $800) ÷ $8,000 = 35%

### Credit

A borrower's credit report shows payment history, balances, inquiries and public records. Under federal law consumers can dispute errors and are entitled to free copies of their reports. A lender that denies credit based on a report must tell the applicant. Brokers should never coach buyers to misstate income or debts — that is mortgage fraud.

> **Exam tip:** "Who does PMI protect?" — always the lender. "What is a point?" — 1% of the loan amount.

lessons.title: Loan types and the secondary market
lessons.body:
## Conventional loans

A **conventional loan** is not insured or guaranteed by a government agency.

- **Conforming** — meets the guidelines of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac (including a maximum loan size set annually), so it can be sold to them.
- **Nonconforming** — doesn't meet those rules. A [[Jumbo loan]] exceeds the conforming loan limit; other nonconforming loans may have credit or documentation features outside the guidelines.

## Repayment structures

- **Fully amortized ([[Amortization]])** — equal payments of principal and interest pay the loan to zero by the end of the term. Early payments are mostly interest; later payments are mostly principal.
- **Partially amortized / [[Balloon payment]]** — payments don't fully retire the loan, so a large lump sum (the balloon) is due at the end.
- **Interest-only** — payments cover just interest for a period; principal is unchanged, so the full principal is still owed afterward.
- **Straight (term) loan** — interest only, with all principal due at maturity.

## Adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs)

An [[Adjustable-rate mortgage]] has a rate that changes after an initial period.

- **[[Index]]** — a published market rate the lender doesn't control. It moves up and down.
- **[[Margin]]** — the lender's fixed markup over the index. It stays the same for the life of the loan.
- **Fully indexed rate = index + margin.**
- **Caps**:
  - *Initial adjustment cap* — limits the first change.
  - *Periodic (adjustment) cap* — limits each later change.
  - *Lifetime cap* — limits the total increase over the life of the loan.
- **[[Negative amortization]]** — if a payment cap keeps payments below the interest due, unpaid interest is added to the balance, so the borrower owes more over time.

**Worked example.** Index 3.25%, margin 2.50%. Fully indexed rate = 5.75%. If the rate was 4.50% and the periodic cap is 1%, the new rate is capped at 5.50% even though the fully indexed rate is 5.75%.

> **Exam tip:** The index changes; the margin does not.

## Government-backed loans

| Program | Who backs it | Key concepts |
|---|---|---|
| **[[FHA loan]]** | Federal Housing Administration (part of HUD) **insures** the lender | Low down payment; mortgage insurance premiums (upfront and annual); property must meet standards; loan limits by county |
| **[[VA loan]]** | Department of Veterans Affairs **guarantees** part of the loan | For eligible veterans and service members; often no down payment; no monthly mortgage insurance; a funding fee usually applies; a Certificate of Eligibility shows entitlement |
| **USDA (Rural Development)** | U.S. Department of Agriculture | Eligible rural areas; income limits; often no down payment |

FHA and VA loans are generally **assumable** by qualified buyers. Neither FHA nor VA lends the money itself in a typical purchase — approved private lenders do. Loan limits and fee percentages change, so learn the concepts.

> **Exam tip:** FHA *insures*; VA *guarantees*.

## Other financing tools

- **Seller financing / purchase-money mortgage** — the seller acts as lender and takes back a note and mortgage or deed of trust for part of the price.
- **[[Land contract]]** (contract for deed, installment contract) — the seller keeps *legal title* until the buyer finishes paying; the buyer gets possession and *equitable title*.
- **[[Wraparound mortgage]]** — a new, larger loan that "wraps" an existing loan; the buyer pays the seller (or wrap lender), who keeps paying the underlying loan. A due-on-sale clause in the underlying loan can block it.
- **[[Reverse mortgage]]** — for older homeowners with substantial equity; the lender pays the owner (lump sum, line or monthly) and the balance *grows*; repaid when the borrower sells, moves out permanently or dies. The federally insured version is the HECM.
- **[[HELOC]]** — home equity line of credit: a revolving line secured by the home, usually in second position. Draw as needed, pay interest on what you use.
- **Construction loan** — short-term loan disbursed in draws as work is completed and inspected; often replaced by a permanent (**takeout**) loan.
- **[[Bridge loan]]** (swing loan) — short-term loan that lets a buyer use equity in the current home to buy the next one before the first one sells.
- **Blanket loan** — one loan secured by several parcels; uses a release clause.
- **Package loan** — covers real property plus personal property (e.g., furniture or appliances).
- **Open-end loan** — lets the borrower borrow more later against the same instrument.
- **Buydown** — someone (often a seller or builder) pays the lender up front to lower the borrower's rate, permanently or for the first years.

## The secondary mortgage market

The **primary market** is where loans are made to borrowers (banks, credit unions, mortgage companies). The **[[Secondary mortgage market]]** is where existing loans are bought and sold, which puts money back in lenders' hands so they can lend again.

| Entity | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Fannie Mae** (FNMA) | Buys conventional (and some government) loans, packages them into securities |
| **Freddie Mac** (FHLMC) | Buys conventional loans, similar role |
| **Ginnie Mae** (GNMA) | Government agency within HUD; **guarantees** securities backed by FHA, VA and other government loans. It does not buy loans |

Uniform loan documents and underwriting standards exist largely so loans can be sold in this market.

> **Exam tip:** Ginnie Mae is the one that stays a government agency and *guarantees* securities of government-backed loans.

lessons.title: Lending laws: RESPA, TILA, TRID and ECOA
lessons.body:
## RESPA — the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act

[[RESPA]] covers most federally related residential mortgage loans on 1–4 unit properties. It is enforced today by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). Its goals: give consumers information about settlement costs and stop practices that inflate them.

### Section 8: kickbacks and unearned fees

RESPA **prohibits giving or accepting any fee, kickback or thing of value in exchange for referring settlement service business** (title, lending, appraisal, inspection, insurance and so on) on a covered loan. It also bars splitting fees when no actual service was performed.

- A broker may **not** take a payment from a lender or title company for sending clients there.
- Cooperative commission splits between brokers are allowed — they pay for real brokerage services.
- Penalties can include fines of up to $10,000 and up to one year in prison per violation, plus civil liability to the consumer for three times the settlement charge involved.

### Affiliated business arrangements

A brokerage may refer clients to a business it has an ownership interest in (say, an affiliated title or mortgage company) **only if**:
1. The consumer gets a written **[[Affiliated business arrangement]] disclosure** describing the relationship and an estimate of charges, at or before the referral;
2. The consumer is **not required** to use the affiliate; and
3. The only thing of value received is a return on ownership interest — not a per-referral fee.

### Other RESPA points

- **Escrow accounts** — limits on how much the lender can collect as a cushion, and annual escrow statements.
- **No seller-required title insurer** — a seller can't require, as a condition of sale, that the buyer use a particular title company.
- **Servicing transfers** — borrowers get notice when servicing moves.

> **Exam tip:** RESPA does not set the interest rate or require any particular lender. It's about disclosure and kickbacks.

## TILA and Regulation Z

The **[[Truth in Lending Act]]** (TILA), implemented by Regulation Z, requires disclosure of the cost of credit so consumers can compare loans. The key number is the **[[Annual percentage rate]] (APR)**, which reflects interest *plus* certain finance charges (such as points and some fees) as a yearly rate. The APR is usually higher than the note rate.

TILA gives a **right of rescission** of three business days on certain refinances and home-equity loans on a principal residence. It does **not** apply to a loan used to buy the home.

### Advertising and trigger terms

If an ad states any **[[Trigger terms]]**, it must include full disclosures. Trigger terms include:
- the amount or percentage of the **down payment**
- the **number of payments** or the period of repayment
- the **amount of any payment**
- the **amount of any finance charge**

Required disclosures when a trigger term is used: the down payment amount or percentage, the terms of repayment, and the APR (including whether it may increase).

General statements like "easy financing," "no down payment," "monthly payments to suit your needs" or simply stating the APR do **not** trigger the full disclosures.

**Worked example.** An ad says "Only $1,850 a month!" — a payment amount is a trigger term, so the ad must also show the down payment, repayment terms and APR.

## TRID — the Know Before You Owe disclosures

[[TRID]] (TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure) combined the old forms into two:

### Loan Estimate

- The creditor must deliver or mail the **[[Loan Estimate]]** no later than the **third business day after it receives the consumer's application**.
- For this purpose an application is six items: name, income, Social Security number (to get a credit report), property address, estimate of property value, and loan amount sought.
- The Loan Estimate must also go out no later than the seventh business day before consummation.

### Closing Disclosure

- The consumer must **receive** the **[[Closing Disclosure]]** at least **three business days before consummation** (the day the borrower becomes contractually obligated on the loan — usually signing at closing).
- If it isn't handed over in person, it's treated as received three business days after it is mailed or delivered, unless proof of earlier receipt exists.
- For the Closing Disclosure waiting period and the seven-business-day Loan Estimate rule, a business day is every calendar day except Sundays and federal legal public holidays. (For the three-day Loan Estimate delivery deadline, a business day is any day the creditor's offices are open for substantially all business functions.)

### Changes that restart the three-day clock

Most changes just require a corrected Closing Disclosure at or before closing. Only **three** changes require a new CD *and* a new three-business-day waiting period:
1. The **APR becomes inaccurate** beyond the allowed tolerance;
2. The **loan product changes** (for example, fixed rate to adjustable);
3. A **prepayment penalty is added**.

> **Exam tip:** A change in the closing date, a seller credit, or a small fee change does not by itself restart the three-day clock. APR, product, prepayment penalty do.

## ECOA — Equal Credit Opportunity Act

The **[[Equal Credit Opportunity Act]]** bars lenders from discriminating in any part of a credit transaction on the basis of:
- race, color, religion, national origin
- sex
- **marital status**
- **age** (if the applicant is old enough to contract)
- receipt of income from **public assistance**
- good-faith exercise of rights under the Consumer Credit Protection Act

Notice that ECOA covers marital status, age and public-assistance income, which the federal Fair Housing Act does not list. Lenders must notify applicants of the action taken on a completed application and, on denial, give the reasons or explain how to get them.

## Risky loan features and predatory lending

Federal rules now require lenders to make a reasonable, good-faith determination of a borrower's **ability to repay** most residential mortgages. A **qualified mortgage** meets stricter standards and generally avoids features like:
- [[Negative amortization]]
- interest-only periods
- balloon payments (with limited exceptions)
- terms longer than 30 years
- excessive points and fees

**Predatory lending** practices to recognize: **loan flipping** (repeated refinancing to generate fees), **equity stripping** (lending based on equity without regard to ability to pay), **packing** (adding unnecessary products like credit insurance), and steering borrowers to costlier loans than they qualify for. **[[Redlining]]** — refusing to lend, or lending on worse terms, in certain neighborhoods because of their racial or ethnic makeup — is illegal under fair lending laws.

> **Exam tip:** If a broker "gets a little something" from a lender or inspector for each referral, that's a RESPA Section 8 violation, even if the consumer pays nothing extra.

lessons.title: Real estate math with worked examples
lessons.body:
## How to attack a math question

1. Read what is actually asked (net to seller? monthly? annual?).
2. Write down the knowns.
3. Pick the formula.
4. Do the arithmetic, then sanity-check the size of the answer.

Most exam math is one of three things: **Part = Whole × Rate**, an area calculation, or a proration.

## Percentages: the Part–Whole–Rate triangle

- Part = Whole × Rate
- Rate = Part ÷ Whole
- Whole = Part ÷ Rate

Convert percentages to decimals: 6% = 0.06, 2.5% = 0.025.

## Commission and splits

**Worked example.** A home sells for $500,000 at 5.5% commission. The listing firm and buyer's firm split 50/50. The buyer's broker gets 70% of her firm's share.
1. Total commission: $500,000 × 0.055 = $27,500
2. Each firm: $27,500 × 0.50 = $13,750
3. Broker's share: $13,750 × 0.70 = **$9,625**

**Working backward.** A seller wants to net $300,000 after a 6% commission (ignore other costs). Price = $300,000 ÷ (1 − 0.06) = $300,000 ÷ 0.94 ≈ **$319,149**. Don't multiply $300,000 by 1.06 — that undershoots because the commission is a percentage of the price, not the net.

## Area and acreage

- Rectangle: length × width. Triangle: ½ × base × height.
- **1 acre = 43,560 sq ft.** A section = 640 acres = 1 square mile. 1 square yard = 9 sq ft.
- Odd shapes: split into rectangles and triangles and add.

**Worked example.** A lot is 330 ft × 660 ft. Area = 217,800 sq ft. Acres = 217,800 ÷ 43,560 = **5 acres**.

## Prorations

[[Proration]] divides an expense or income between buyer and seller as of closing.

- **Statutory/banker's year (360 days)**: every month is 30 days. Daily rate = annual ÷ 360, or monthly ÷ 30.
- **Calendar year (365 days)**: actual days. Daily rate = annual ÷ 365.
- Who "owns" the day of closing varies by contract and local custom. The question will tell you; if the seller owns it, count it in the seller's days.

### Debit and credit logic

A **[[Debit]]** is money a party owes at closing; a **[[Credit]]** is money a party receives.

| Situation | Seller | Buyer |
|---|---|---|
| Taxes paid in **arrears**, unpaid at closing | Debit (owes their share) | Credit |
| Expense **prepaid** by seller | Credit (refund for unused days) | Debit |
| Rent collected in advance by seller | Debit (unearned portion) | Credit |
| Purchase price | Credit | Debit |
| New loan | — | Credit |
| Earnest money | — | Credit |
| Seller's payoff of existing loan | Debit | — |

**Worked example — taxes in arrears (360-day year).** Annual taxes $2,700, not yet paid. Closing June 15; seller owns through June 14.
1. Daily rate: $2,700 ÷ 360 = $7.50
2. Seller's days: 5 months × 30 + 14 = 164 days
3. Seller's share: 164 × $7.50 = **$1,230** → debit seller, credit buyer

**Same thing with a 365-day year.** Days Jan 1–June 14 = 31+28+31+30+31+14 = 165. $2,700 ÷ 365 × 165 ≈ **$1,220.55**.

## Seller's net proceeds

**Net = Sales price − all seller debits** (loan payoff, commission, seller-paid closing costs, prorated debits) **+ seller credits** (prepaid items).

**Worked example.** Price $400,000; commission 6% ($24,000); loan payoff $250,000; seller closing costs $3,500; tax proration debit $1,200.
Net = $400,000 − $24,000 − $250,000 − $3,500 − $1,200 = **$121,300**.

## Buyer's cash to close

**Cash to close = Price + buyer costs + buyer debits − loan − earnest money − other buyer credits.**

**Worked example.** Price $400,000; 80% loan ($320,000); buyer closing costs $6,000; 1 point on the loan ($3,200); earnest money $10,000; tax proration credit $1,200.
1. Down payment: $400,000 − $320,000 = $80,000
2. Add costs and points: $80,000 + $6,000 + $3,200 = $89,200
3. Subtract earnest money and credit: $89,200 − $10,000 − $1,200 = **$78,000**

## LTV and points

- [[LTV]] = Loan ÷ lesser of price or appraised value.
- Loan = Value × LTV.
- **1 point = 1% of the loan amount.**

**Worked example.** Price $350,000; 90% LTV; 2 points. Loan = $315,000. Points = $315,000 × 0.02 = **$6,300**.

## Investment math

- **[[Cap rate]]** = NOI ÷ Value; Value = NOI ÷ Cap rate; NOI = Value × Cap rate. Remember **I-R-V**: Income = Rate × Value.
- **Rate of return** (simple) = annual profit or income ÷ amount invested.
- **[[Equity]]** = Market value − Loan balance(s).

**Worked example.** NOI $72,000, cap rate 8%. Value = $72,000 ÷ 0.08 = **$900,000**. If the cap rate rises to 9%, value drops to $800,000.

## Interest and amortization

**Simple interest = Principal × Rate × Time.** $20,000 at 6% for 1 year = $1,200.

Monthly interest on an amortized loan = balance × annual rate ÷ 12.

**Worked example — first payment.** $200,000 loan, 6%, 30 years, monthly P&I $1,199.10.
1. Interest for month 1: $200,000 × 0.06 ÷ 12 = $1,000
2. Principal: $1,199.10 − $1,000 = $199.10
3. New balance: $200,000 − $199.10 = **$199,800.90**

Next month's interest is a little lower because the balance is lower — that's [[Amortization]].

## Appreciation and depreciation

- **Appreciation:** New value = Original × (1 + rate). Loss: New value = Original × (1 − rate).
- **Percent change** = (New − Old) ÷ Old.
- **Straight-line depreciation** (building only): Annual = Cost of improvement ÷ economic life.

**Worked example.** A home bought for $300,000 is now worth $345,000. Change = $45,000 ÷ $300,000 = **15% appreciation**.

**Trap:** a property that is worth $180,000 after losing 10% was originally $180,000 ÷ 0.90 = $200,000 — not $198,000.

## Property tax via mill levy

A **[[Mill levy]]** is a tax rate in mills. **1 mill = $1 of tax per $1,000 of assessed value** (= 0.001).

**Tax = Assessed value × mill levy ÷ 1,000.**

In Colorado, the assessed value is the county assessor's actual value multiplied by an assessment rate set by law; that rate changes, so the exam gives you the numbers.

**Worked example.** Assessed value $30,000; total mill levy 85 mills.
$30,000 × 85 ÷ 1,000 = **$2,550** per year.

> **Exam tip:** If you get an answer that's wildly off (a $4 million commission on a starter home), you probably misplaced a decimal. Re-check before moving on.

lessons.title: Federal income tax and real estate
lessons.body:
