Cash, debt relief or other non-like-kind property received in an exchange. Gain is taxable up to the boot.
Holds the exchange proceeds so the investor never controls the cash. The investor's own agent or broker generally can't serve.
At least one payment is received after the year of sale; gain is reported proportionally as payments come in.

cards.front: Federal tax lien vs property tax lien
cards.back: IRS lien is general (all property); property tax lien is specific (one parcel). A property tax lien with priority under local law stays ahead even of an earlier-filed federal tax lien.
Generally fair market value on the date of death.

cards.front: Broker's role on client tax questions
cards.back: Recognize the issue and refer the client to a CPA or tax attorney; don't give tax advice.
Funds released in stages as work is completed and inspected; interest usually paid only on amounts drawn.
The permanent long-term loan that pays off the interim construction loan when the building is finished.
One loan (usually one closing) that funds construction and then converts to a permanent mortgage.
The Appraisal Standards Board of The Appraisal Foundation.
Sets minimum education, experience and exam criteria for appraisers; states license and certify using them.
Trainee → licensed residential → certified residential → certified general (all property types).
Allowed: give comps, ask to correct errors or explain. Prohibited: requesting a target value, tying pay or future work to the value.
Association of Real Estate License Law Officials — an association of license-law regulators. It licenses no one.

cards.front: Five essential elements of a real estate contract
cards.back: Competent parties, offer and acceptance, consideration, legal purpose, and a writing (Statute of Frauds).
Requires contracts for the sale of real property (and, in many states, leases over one year) to be in writing and signed to be enforceable.
Promise for a promise; both parties bound. Example: purchase contract.
Promise for an act; only one party bound. Example: option before exercise.
Express: terms stated in words (oral or written). Implied: created by the parties' conduct.
Executory: obligations remain. Executed: fully performed (e.g., after closing).
No legal effect at all. Examples: illegal purpose; party previously adjudicated incompetent.
Valid until the protected party disaffirms. Examples: minor's contract; fraud, duress, undue influence.
Appears valid but a court won't enforce it — e.g., an oral real estate sales contract or one past the statute of limitations.
Voidable by the minor only; the adult stays bound.
Fraud is intentional deception about a material fact; misrepresentation can be innocent or negligent. Both can make a contract voidable.
Duress: threats or force. Undue influence: abusing a position of trust or control.
Mutual mistake of a material fact can void a contract; a one-sided mistake usually doesn't.
Vague opinion or exaggeration ("best view in town"); not misrepresentation because it isn't a statement of fact.
Something of legal value exchanged — money or a promise. Earnest money isn't required; the promise to pay is consideration.
Rejects and ends the original offer and creates a new offer with roles reversed.

cards.front: When can an offer be revoked?
cards.back: Any time before acceptance is communicated to the offeror, even if it says it will stay open (unless it's an option).
Acceptance, rejection, counteroffer, revocation, expiration, death or incapacity of a party, destruction of the property.
When the unconditional acceptance is communicated (delivered) to the offeror or the offeror's agent.
Acceptance must match the offer exactly; any change makes it a counteroffer.
Present all offers promptly; the seller decides. Don't share terms with other buyers without seller permission.
Give electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper when parties agree to transact electronically.
Optionee pays for the right (not obligation) to buy at a set price within a set time; optionor must sell if exercised.
Optionor = owner who grants the option and is bound. Optionee = holder of the right to buy.
Right to match a third-party offer if the owner decides to sell. No set price; owner can't be forced to sell.
Assignment: assignor stays secondarily liable. Novation: new contract/party; original party released.

cards.front: Can a listing agreement be assigned?
cards.back: Generally no without consent — it's a personal service contract with the broker.
Condition that must be satisfied before a party must perform (financing, appraisal, inspection, sale of home).
Makes contract deadlines strict; missing one is a breach.
Addendum: added when the contract is signed. Amendment: changes the contract after formation; all parties sign.
Court order to perform as promised; mainly a buyer's remedy because land is unique.
Damages amount agreed in advance; commonly the earnest money. Must be reasonable, not a penalty.
Money to cover the actual loss caused by a breach.
Cancels the contract and returns parties to their original positions.
Deadline to file suit; after it runs the claim is unenforceable. Length varies by state.
Performance, mutual release, novation, impossibility, operation of law, breach.
The buyer's interest under a signed purchase contract before closing; seller still holds legal title.
Lease with a definite beginning and end; ends automatically, no notice needed.
Renews automatically period to period (e.g., month-to-month) until proper notice.

cards.front: Tenancy at will vs. at sufferance
cards.back: At will: no set term, both consent, ends on notice or death. At sufferance: holdover without landlord consent.
Gross: landlord pays property expenses. Net: tenant pays some or all (triple net = taxes, insurance, maintenance).
Base rent plus a percentage of gross sales, often over a threshold; typical in retail.
Ground: land only, tenant builds. Graduated: scheduled step increases. Index: rent tied to an index such as CPI.
Lease option: tenant may buy. Lease-purchase: tenant agrees to buy.

cards.front: Assignment vs. sublease of a lease
cards.back: Assignment: entire remaining interest; assignee pays landlord. Sublease: part of interest; subtenant pays original tenant.
A fact that would affect a reasonable buyer's decision or the price paid.
Latent: hidden, not found by ordinary inspection — must be disclosed if known. Patent: visible on reasonable inspection.
Property with a psychological stigma (death, crime, illness) but no physical defect. Colorado: not a material fact requiring disclosure (C.R.S. 38-35.5-101).
Most housing built before 1978.
10 days to inspect or do a risk assessment; may be changed by written agreement or waived.
3 years after closing or the start of the lease.
Protect Your Family From Lead in Your Home.
EPA: fix the home at 4 pCi/L or higher.
Crumbling asbestos that releases fibers — the dangerous condition. Intact asbestos is often left or encapsulated.
Strict, joint and several, and retroactive; current owners can be liable for past contamination.
Review of past uses and records to identify possible contamination; supports CERCLA defenses.
Protected under the Clean Water Act; filling usually requires an Army Corps of Engineers permit.
FEMA zone (A or V) with 1% annual flood chance; flood insurance required with federally backed loans.

cards.front: Broker response to a suspected hazard
cards.back: Disclose what you observed and recommend an expert inspection.
Client (principal) = represented, owed fiduciary duties. Customer = unrepresented third party, owed honesty and disclosure.
Express (words), implied (conduct), ratification (approval after the fact), estoppel (principal's conduct led others to believe it).
Principal approves, after the fact, an act the agent did without authority.
Principal's words or conduct led a third party to reasonably believe an agency existed, so the principal can't deny it.
No. A broker acting for free can still owe fiduciary duties.

cards.front: Does who pays the commission decide who the agent represents?
cards.back: No. Representation comes from the agency agreement, not the source of the fee.
Authority for one specific act or transaction. Example: listing broker, buyer's broker.
Authority over a range of acts in one business. Example: property manager.
Broad authority to do anything the principal could delegate, e.g., under a general power of attorney.
Broker paid no matter who sells during the term, even the owner.
One broker; owner can sell on their own and owe no commission.
Several brokers; only the procuring cause is paid; owner selling alone pays nobody.
Broker keeps everything above the seller's net figure. Banned in many states; Colorado has no approved form, and secret profits are grounds for discipline.
The broker whose efforts started the unbroken chain of events that produced the sale.
Broker can still earn a fee if the owner sells, after the listing ends, to a buyer the broker introduced during the term.

cards.front: Ways agency ends by operation of law
cards.back: Death or incapacity of either party, destruction or condemnation of property, bankruptcy, change in law.
Agent holds a stake in the property; the principal can't revoke it, and it survives the principal's death.
Survives the principal's incapacity but ends at death.
Obedience, Loyalty, Disclosure, Confidentiality, Accounting, Reasonable care.
Follow only lawful instructions. Refuse illegal (e.g., discriminatory) ones.
Disclosure: tell your client everything material. Confidentiality: keep the client's private info from others.
Honesty, fair dealing, reasonable care, disclosure of known material (latent) defects.
Exaggerated opinion or sales talk ("stunning view"). Not usually actionable.
False statement of fact the licensee should have known was false.
Where allowed: informed, written consent of both parties. Undisclosed dual agency is illegal everywhere. Colorado prohibits dual agency entirely.
Employing broker assigns different licensees in the same firm to buyer and seller, each with full duties to their client.
Assists one or both parties without advocacy; duties set by state statute. Colorado has its own rules (see Colorado module).
Disclose license status and personal interest in writing first; never use a straw buyer.
Race only; NO exemptions; enforced directly in federal court. Revived by Jones v. Mayer (1968).
Race, color, religion, national origin, sex, disability, familial status.

cards.front: When were sex, disability and familial status added?
cards.back: Sex: 1974. Disability and familial status: 1988 amendments.
Child under 18 living with parent/custodian/designee; includes pregnancy and someone gaining custody.

cards.front: Sexual orientation / gender identity under federal FHA
cards.back: Not listed in the Act. HUD's 2021 memo treating them as sex discrimination was withdrawn on Sept. 17, 2025. Colorado law expressly protects them.
Directing buyers/renters toward or away from areas based on a protected class.
Inducing owners to sell by suggesting a protected class is moving in. Also called panic peddling.
Lender refuses or limits loans in an area because of its racial/ethnic makeup.
Owner of max 3 homes, no broker, no discriminatory ads; one non-occupant sale per 24 months.
Owner-occupied building with up to four units living independently.
At least 80% of occupied units have a resident 55+, published policies, age verification. Exempt from familial status only.
Accommodation = change in rules/policies (provider bears cost). Modification = physical change (tenant pays in private housing).
HUD complaint: 1 year. Private lawsuit: 2 years.
Public accommodations and commercial facilities, e.g., brokerage and leasing offices. Not private dwelling units.
Price fixing, group boycotts, market allocation, tie-in arrangements.
Licensed; pay based on sales output; written agreement saying not an employee for tax purposes.
Scrub every 31 days; call 8 a.m.-9 p.m.; EBR 18 months after transaction / 3 months after inquiry; honor company DNC 5 years.
Honor within 10 business days; opt-out must work 30 days after sending; include physical postal address.
Commingling: mixing client and broker funds. Conversion: using client funds for yourself.

cards.front: What unlicensed assistants may NOT do
cards.back: Show property, negotiate, discuss terms, host open houses alone, or be paid per closing for licensed activity.
Best net operating income for the owner, and preserving/increasing property value.
Percentage of gross rents collected (sometimes plus leasing fees).
Preventive: prevent problems (best protects value). Corrective: fix what's broken.
Avoid, Control, Transfer (insurance), Retain.
Actual: tenant removed by legal process. Constructive: landlord makes unit unusable and tenant moves out.
Tenant's right to use the premises without interference by the landlord or someone with superior title.

cards.back: Registers HOAs, educates owners and logs complaints. It doesn't investigate, mediate, fine or enforce.

cards.front: When can an HOA foreclose its assessment lien under CCIOA?
cards.back: When the balance equals or exceeds 6 months of common-expense assessments and the board has authorized action against that unit by recorded vote. Fines alone can't be foreclosed.
No more than two months' rent, held by the buyer and returned within 30 days after the term.

cards.front: Who is responsible for the proper closing of a Colorado transaction when a title company closes?
cards.back: The broker with the brokerage relationship; using a closing company doesn't remove that responsibility.

cards.front: What must the consumer receive from the broker at closing?
cards.back: An accurate, complete and detailed closing statement signed by the broker.

cards.front: Broker can't attend closing — what then?
cards.back: A firm-designated broker may attend and shares (joint) responsibility for the statement's accuracy, completeness and delivery.

cards.front: Failing to give buyer and seller a closing statement violates which statute?
cards.back: C.R.S. 12-10-217(1)(j) — a ground for license discipline.

cards.front: Who signs the Commission's Closing Instructions?
cards.back: Buyer, seller and closing company. Brokers are not parties.
C.R.S. 38-35-125: no disbursement until funds are received and available for immediate withdrawal (wire, cashier's/certified/teller's check).
Closing statement: required by Colorado license law in every deal. Closing Disclosure: federal TRID form for most consumer mortgage loans.
One cent per $100 of consideration; none if consideration is $500 or less.
The county clerk and recorder, when the deed is recorded.
Real Property Transfer Declaration: reports sale price to the assessor; filed with the deed; confidential.
Race-notice: an unrecorded deed loses to a later buyer who records first without notice.

cards.front: Default title company selection in the CBS1 contract
cards.back: If neither box is checked, the seller selects the title company and pays for the owner's policy.
Deletes standard exceptions (e.g., unrecorded mechanics' liens, survey matters); contract says if it applies and who pays.

cards.front: When are Colorado property taxes due?
cards.back: January 1 of the year after they're levied — paid in arrears.
In full by the end of April, or in halves by the end of February and June 15.
Debit seller, credit buyer for the seller's share.
Taxes for the calendar year immediately before closing, with most recent mill levy and assessed valuation.

cards.front: Rent collected in advance by seller
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer for the buyer's days.
Transferred in full: debit seller, credit buyer. Not prorated.
Credit seller, debit buyer for the buyer's days.

cards.front: Are HOA reserves credited to the seller at closing?
cards.back: No, unless the governing documents say otherwise.

cards.front: Association status letter timing and cost
cards.back: Seller requests it at least 14 days before closing; seller pays the status letter fee.
Lesser of 2% of price or net proceeds; not when price is $100,000 or less, or with residency/principal-residence affirmation.

cards.front: Who needs a license to manage rentals for others in Colorado?
cards.back: Anyone leasing/renting for another for compensation — except a salaried on-site manager of an apartment/condo owner doing customary duties.
Separate accounts for rents and security deposits; deposit within 5 business days.
Two months' rent.
One month after lease end/surrender, or longer if the lease says so — max 60 days.
Treble damages plus fees; tenant gives 7 days' notice before suing.
Respond within 24 hours of notice; begin remedial action within 24 hours (life/health/safety) or 96 hours (other uninhabitable conditions, with permission to enter).

cards.front: Residential notice for nonpayment or lease violation
cards.back: 10 days (5 for exempt small-landlord leases; 3 for nonresidential/employer housing).

cards.front: Can a landlord change locks or shut off utilities to evict?
cards.back: No — removal requires court process (C.R.S. 38-12-510).
Landlord generally needs cause to evict or refuse to renew a tenant who has lived there 12+ months; no-fault grounds need ~90 days' notice. Check current law.
Prior appropriation: first in time, first in right.
With the same formalities as real estate, usually by recorded deed; ditch company shares by stock assignment.
Buyer acknowledges Seller's Property Disclosure or Source of Water Addendum and, if a well, the current well permit.

cards.front: Who files the well change-in-ownership form?
cards.back: Buyer completes it; closing company submits it to Division of Water Resources within 60 days after closing.
Water-court-approved plan replacing a well's stream depletions so senior rights aren't injured.
Actual value x assessment rate = assessed value; assessed value x mill levy (mills/1,000) = tax.
Bold notice in every residential contract: districts may have debt and raise mill levies; seller's duty.
Seller gives buyer the district's official website (districts organized on/after Jan 1, 2000).
FIRPTA: foreign-person sellers (IRS). Colorado: nonresident sellers (Dept. of Revenue).
Creed, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, marital status, ancestry, veteran/military status, source of income.

cards.front: Deadline to file a housing charge with the CCRD
cards.back: Within one year of the alleged discriminatory act.
The county public trustee, under a deed of trust (non-judicial).
110–125 days after the notice of election and demand is recorded.
Notice of intent to cure 15+ calendar days before sale; pay by noon the day before sale.
Junior lienors only; owner has no post-sale redemption. Intent to redeem within 8 business days.
Protects homeowners in foreclosure from equity-stripping by foreclosure consultants and equity purchasers.

cards.front: Is a broker a foreclosure consultant?
cards.back: Not while acting within the license; but an investor-broker can be an equity purchaser.
Can't be collected until every promised service is fully performed.
Until midnight of the 3rd business day after signing or noon the day before the sale, whichever is first.

cards.front: When can't the CFPA contract be used?
cards.back: Seller leaseback, seller repurchase right, or buyer assuming the loan — an attorney must draft.

cards.front: On a six-column settlement worksheet, what are the three column pairs?
cards.back: Seller debit/credit, buyer debit/credit, and broker (cash) debit/credit.

cards.front: In the broker (cash) column, what does a debit mean? A credit?
cards.back: Debit = money received into the closing. Credit = money paid out.

cards.front: What is a double entry on a closing worksheet?
cards.back: An item between buyer and seller: one is debited and the other credited the same amount, usually with no cash entry.

cards.front: What is a single entry on a closing worksheet?
cards.back: An item between one party and an outsider (lender, county, title company, brokerage); it hits that party's column and the cash column.
Buyer credit; cash debit (received). Never a seller entry.
Buyer credit; cash debit. The seller's side is not affected.

cards.front: Payoff of the seller's loan: worksheet entries?
cards.back: Seller debit; cash credit (paid to the seller's lender).
Debit seller, credit buyer. No cash moves.
Debit seller, credit buyer. The seller takes a note instead of cash; no cash entry.

cards.front: Accrued interest on an assumed loan (paid in arrears)?
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer for the seller's days; the buyer's next payment covers them.

cards.front: Lender escrow reserve that transfers with an assumed loan?
cards.back: Credit seller, debit buyer (the seller funded it; the buyer gets it).

cards.front: Unpaid current-year Colorado property taxes at closing?
cards.back: Seller's share: debit seller, credit buyer. Colorado taxes are paid in arrears.

cards.front: Unpaid prior-year Colorado taxes at closing?
cards.back: Seller debit for the full amount, paid out to the county treasurer. Not prorated.

cards.front: Rent the seller collected for days after closing?
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer for the buyer's days.

cards.front: Tenant security deposits when leases are assigned?
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer for the full amount. Not prorated.

cards.front: Seller concession toward the buyer's closing costs?
cards.back: Debit seller, credit buyer.

cards.front: Who pays the owner's title policy if neither box is checked in the Colorado contract?
cards.back: The seller (who also selects the title company).

cards.front: Colorado documentary fee: rate and worksheet entry?
cards.back: $0.01 per $100 of consideration (none at $500 or less), on the full price. The contract doesn't assign it: debit whichever party the problem says pays, and credit cash.

cards.front: How is the balance due to the seller entered?
cards.back: Seller debit (to balance the seller columns) and cash credit (paid out).

cards.front: How is the balance due from the buyer entered?
cards.back: Buyer credit (to balance the buyer columns) and cash debit (received).

cards.front: Quick formula: seller's cash at closing?
cards.back: Seller credits − seller debits.

cards.front: Quick formula: buyer's cash to close?
cards.back: Buyer debits − buyer credits.

cards.front: Cash column won't balance but both party pairs do. Likely cause?
cards.back: A single-entry item is missing its cash entry (or a cash entry is missing its party entry).

cards.front: Does a lender's Closing Disclosure satisfy the Colorado broker's closing statement duty?
cards.back: No. The broker who works with a party must still see that the party gets an accurate, complete closing statement signed by the broker.

glossary.definition: A condensed history of all recorded documents affecting a property, usually reviewed by an attorney.
Loan provision letting the lender declare the entire balance due on default.
The offeree's unconditional agreement to the exact terms of an offer, communicated to the offeror.
A formal declaration before a notary or other officer that a signature is genuine and voluntary. Most states require it before a deed can be recorded.
A unit of land area equal to 43,560 square feet.
Removal of a tenant by the landlord through legal process.
What a person actually knows, from seeing, hearing, or reading it.
The assessor's market-based value of property for property tax purposes.
Additional material attached to and made part of a contract when it is signed.
The section of a Commission form where negotiated, transaction-specific terms are written. This language is not Commission-approved and must not amount to the broker practicing law.
A loan whose interest rate changes periodically based on an index plus a margin, within caps.
Basis increased by capital improvements and reduced by depreciation and casualty losses; subtracted from the amount realized to find gain.
A judge who conducts formal disciplinary and license-denial hearings for the Commission under the state Administrative Procedure Act.
A fact a reasonable person would consider significant that works against a party's interest. Brokers must disclose those they actually know.
Gaining title to another's land by open, notorious, continuous, exclusive, and hostile possession for the statutory period.
A situation where a broker or firm has an ownership interest in a settlement service provider it refers business to; requires disclosure to consumers and the Commission.
A relationship in which one person (the agent) is authorized to act for another (the principal) in dealings with third parties.
Agency found when a principal's words or conduct led a third party to reasonably believe someone was their agent.
A person or firm authorized to act on behalf of a principal.
The Commission form, signed by both parties, used to change deadlines or other terms of a signed contract.
Loan provision letting the lender call the loan due if the property is sold or transferred.
A negotiated later date for delivering earnest money, instead of delivering it with the contract.
A change to the terms of an existing contract, signed by all parties after the contract is formed.
Federal disability law; Title III requires public accommodations and commercial facilities to be accessible.
Paying down a loan with regular payments of principal and interest so the balance reaches zero by the end of the term.
The sale price minus selling expenses such as commission and seller-paid closing costs.
The 4-hour course the Commission issues each year that every active broker must complete; three versions count for 12 of the 24 CE hours per cycle.
The yearly cost of credit, including interest and certain finance charges such as points.
Federal laws, mainly the Sherman Act, that prohibit agreements restraining competition.
A formal, unbiased opinion of value prepared by a state-licensed or certified appraiser.
The board of The Appraisal Foundation that writes and interprets USPAP.
The board of The Appraisal Foundation that sets minimum education, experience and exam criteria for appraiser credentials.
A right or improvement that belongs to the land and passes with it on transfer, such as an easement appurtenant.
Association of Real Estate License Law Officials — an association of government real estate regulators that supports license-law administration; it does not license anyone.
aliases: Association of Real Estate License Law Officials

glossary.definition: A fibrous mineral once used in building materials that is hazardous when friable (crumbling).
Actual value times the assessment rate; the value the mill levy is applied to.
Percentage set by law that converts actual value into assessed value.
Owners' shares of a common interest community's common expenses, allocated by the declaration and secured by a statutory lien.
Transfer of a party's contract rights (and usually duties) to another; the assignor stays secondarily liable.
A Commission optional form a landlord-seller uses to transfer existing leases and security deposits to the buyer at closing. The buyer assumes the landlord's obligations.
A Colorado broker working under the supervision of an employing broker; the level every new licensee starts at.
The owners' association's governing documents, insurance list, assessments, financial records and construction-defect notices that the seller provides to the buyer.
Water-court-approved plan that replaces depletions from well pumping so senior water rights aren't injured.
A computer model that estimates value from sales and public-record data without an inspection.
The buyer's debits minus credits: the cash the buyer must bring to closing.
The seller's credits minus debits: the cash the seller receives at closing.
A large lump sum due at the end of a partially amortized or interest-only loan.
A deed that implies the grantor holds title but gives no express warranties against encumbrances.
A property owner's starting tax investment, usually the purchase price plus certain acquisition costs.
A contract in which each party exchanges a promise and both are obligated.
Inducing owners to sell by suggesting that members of a protected class are moving into the area.
In an oil and gas lease, the one-time payment made to the mineral owner when the lease is signed.
Cash, debt relief or other non-like-kind property received in an exchange; gain is taxable up to the amount of boot.
Failure to perform a contract promise without legal excuse.
The gross sales level above which percentage rent is owed; the natural breakpoint equals annual base rent divided by the percentage rate.
A short-term loan that lets a buyer use equity in a current home to buy a new one before the first sells.
A broker's estimate of value, often ordered by a lender or asset manager; it is not an appraisal.

The written statement of the broker's relationship with a party, required before confidential information is discussed. It is made in a signed engagement contract or on a Commission brokerage disclosure form (to buyer, tenant, seller or landlord).
The Commission's Brokerage Duties Addendum to Property Management Agreement. It attaches to an attorney-drafted management agreement and sets out the brokerage relationship and duties.
aliases: Brokerage Duties Addendum to Property Management Agreement

glossary.definition: Local standards for construction, plumbing, electrical, and fire safety, enforced through permits and inspections.
A transfer of a major part of a business's inventory or equipment outside the ordinary course of business, which in some states triggers notice requirements.
The set of legal rights that come with owning real property: possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition.
A scam in which criminals hack or imitate a legitimate email account to trick recipients into sending money or information.
The sale or lease of an operating business, including its assets, inventory and goodwill.
A relationship in which the broker represents the buyer as a client.
A single agent who represents only the buyer. In leasing, the tenant's agent plays the same role.
The association's rules for running itself: board, elections, officers and meetings.
Federal law governing commercial email, requiring accurate headers, a postal address and a working opt-out.
The legal ability to enter a contract: being of legal age and mentally competent.
Profit from selling a capital asset; long-term if held more than one year, short-term if held one year or less.
Additions or upgrades that add value, prolong useful life or adapt property to new uses; they increase basis, unlike ordinary repairs.
The rate used to convert net operating income into value: value = NOI ÷ cap rate.
"Let the buyer beware" — the old rule that buyers must discover defects themselves.
The Commission's Contract to Buy and Sell Real Estate (Residential) (Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act). It is for buying an owner-occupied home in foreclosure when the buyer won't live there.
Covenants, conditions, and restrictions recorded for a subdivision or condominium that bind all owners.
A formal public reprimand imposed as discipline.
The Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act (Superfund), imposing strict, joint and several, retroactive cleanup liability.
aliases: Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation, and Liability Act

glossary.definition: Document given to the winning bidder at a public trustee sale, later exchanged for a confirmation deed.
The state-issued title document for a manufactured home that hasn't been converted to real property. It transfers ownership instead of a deed.
The recorded history of conveyances from the original source of title to the current owner.
Commission-approved disclosure given when a broker moves from single agent for one party to transaction-broker for both, no later than when the consumer signs the contract.
Federal law prohibiting all racial discrimination in property transactions, with no exemptions.
Common term for a party who has engaged the broker as a single agent or transaction-broker.
The title company or other settlement provider that prepares closing figures, collects and disburses funds, and records documents.
Federal TRID form giving a borrower final loan terms and closing costs, for most consumer mortgage loans.
The Commission form signed by buyer, seller and closing company that engages the closing company to prepare documents, close and disburse funds.
An itemized accounting of each party's debits and credits at closing; Colorado requires brokers to ensure parties receive an accurate one signed by the broker.
A claim or document that casts doubt on title, such as an unreleased lien or a possible heir's claim.
Cooperation between two brokerages on one transaction, with the commission split set by agreement.
State agency that investigates discrimination complaints, including housing.

C.R.S. 38-33.3, the statute governing Colorado common interest communities and their associations. It applies to communities created on or after July 1, 1992, and only listed sections apply to older ones.
Colorado's housing discrimination law (C.R.S. 24-34-501 et seq.), covering more protected classes than federal law.
Law (C.R.S. 6-1-1101 et seq.) protecting homeowners in foreclosure from foreclosure consultants and equity purchasers.
The five-member, governor-appointed board that makes rules for Colorado brokers, approves standard forms, and decides disciplinary cases.
Mixing a broker's or firm's own money with money belonging to others. Prohibited.
A compensation model in which the firm keeps an agreed share of each commission and pays the rest to the broker.
A standard contract or form promulgated by the Commission; brokers must use it when one exists and fits the transaction.
Costs of operating and maintaining shared areas of a multi-tenant property, passed through to tenants by their pro rata shares.
Real estate where owning a unit or lot obligates the owner to pay for common elements or other units' expenses. Examples are condos, townhome communities and HOA subdivisions.

The bold-type statement C.R.S. 38-35.7-102 requires in contracts for residential property in a CIC. It covers membership, assessments, liens, architectural approval and the buyer's need to investigate.
A system in some states under which property acquired during marriage is owned equally by both spouses. Colorado is not a community property state.
Recently sold properties similar to the subject, used in the sales comparison approach and adjusted toward the subject.
A broker's estimate of a property's likely price based on recent sales, listings and expired listings of similar properties.
Having the experience, training and knowledge needed for a particular brokerage task, and keeping up with the laws that apply to it.
Permission for a use the zoning ordinance allows only under specified conditions, such as a church in a residential zone.
Ownership of an individual unit in fee simple plus an undivided interest in common elements shared with other owners.
A real or apparent personal or professional interest that could affect a broker's duties to a client; must be disclosed in writing.
A recorded, usually permanent restriction on development that the owner grants to a land trust or government agency while keeping ownership.
Something of legal value — money, property, or a promise — exchanged by each party to a contract.
A short-term interim loan that funds building improvements, paid out in draws as work is completed.
A single loan, usually with one closing, that funds construction and then converts to a permanent mortgage.
A landlord's act or neglect that makes premises unusable, allowing the tenant to leave and end the lease.
Notice the law presumes everyone has, from public records or from inspecting the property.
A condition that must be met before a party is obligated to perform under a contract.
Principle that a component's value equals what it adds to the whole property, not its cost.
Using money belonging to others for the broker's own purposes or for a different beneficiary.
The 1957 Colorado Supreme Court case allowing brokers to fill in standard forms in their own transactions without charging beyond their commission.
aliases: Conway-Bogue Realty v. Denver Bar Association

glossary.definition: Ownership in which a corporation holds title to a building and residents own shares plus a proprietary lease for their units.
Repairs to something that has already broken.

Tax depreciation: the annual deduction that recovers the cost of buildings used in business or held for investment (27.5 years residential rental, 39 years nonresidential, straight-line); land isn't depreciable. Unlike appraisal depreciation, it isn't an actual loss in value.
A response that changes an offer's terms; it rejects the original offer and becomes a new offer.
The Commission form used to respond to an offer with changed terms. It supersedes earlier counterproposals and expires without timely notice of acceptance.
An amount in a party's favor on a closing statement — something they receive or have already paid.
Paying past-due amounts and costs before the sale to stop a foreclosure and reinstate the loan.
A party to a transaction who has not engaged the broker, so the broker has no brokerage relationship with that party.
The table near the front of a Colorado contract that lists every deadline (title, inspection, loan, appraisal, closing, possession) as a date or a number of days after MEC.
A charge to a party on a closing statement — something they owe.
The recorded document that creates a common interest community. It defines units and common elements, allocates assessments and sets restrictions.
A written instrument that conveys title to real property from a grantor to a grantee.
A borrower's voluntary conveyance of the property to the lender to avoid foreclosure.
The security instrument used in Colorado. The borrower conveys title to the county Public Trustee as security for the lender's note.
A private limit on property use written into a deed or recorded declaration.
Provision requiring the lender to release the lien once the debt is fully paid.

Commission-approved form defining seller's agent, buyer's agent, transaction-broker and customer. Required when a party asks about a relationship the firm doesn't offer. Its definitions alone are not the brokerage disclosure, and it is not a contract.
A payment that keeps an oil and gas lease in force during the primary term when drilling has not started.
Written notice a landlord must give before filing eviction, usually 10 days for residential tenants in Colorado.
In appraisal, any loss in value from any cause: physical deterioration, functional obsolescence or external obsolescence.
Taxing, at sale, the part of a gain that came from depreciation deductions taken during ownership.
An arrangement in which the employing broker assigns different licensees in the same firm to represent the buyer and the seller.
A broker the employing broker designates in writing to work with a particular party. The relationship does not extend to the employing broker, other brokers or the firm.
A fixed fee a broker pays the firm (monthly or per transaction) in exchange for keeping most or all of each commission.
Prepaid interest paid to lower a loan's rate; one point equals 1% of the loan amount.
The state agency within the Department of Regulatory Agencies that staffs the Commission, investigates complaints, audits brokers, and enforces the license law.
The national list of phone numbers that telemarketers may not call without an exception; checked at least every 31 days.
Colorado state fee of one cent per $100 of consideration, collected by the county clerk and recorder when a deed is recorded.
A closing item that passes between buyer and seller, debited to one and credited to the other in the same amount.
Staged disbursements of a construction loan, released after the lender verifies completed work.
One broker acting as agent for both sides of a transaction. Prohibited in Colorado by statute.
A copy of a document, including a photocopy, fax or electronic copy with electronic signatures.
Forcing a person to agree through threats or force; makes a contract voidable.
Federal law (2000) giving electronic signatures and records the same legal effect as paper ones.
aliases: Electronic Signatures in Global and National Commerce Act

glossary.definition: A buyer's good-faith deposit under a purchase contract, held in trust for both parties.
The party named in the contract to hold the earnest money, usually the listing brokerage or a title company.
The Commission form, signed by buyer and seller, that directs how earnest money is paid out and mutually releases the parties.
A non-possessory right to use another person's land for a specific purpose.
An easement that benefits a neighboring (dominant) parcel and burdens the servient parcel. It runs with the land.
An easement that benefits a person or company rather than a neighboring parcel, such as a utility line easement.
An electronic mark or process adopted to sign a record. Under Colorado's UETA it satisfies a legal signature requirement.
Annual crops produced by labor. They're treated as personal property, and a tenant farmer may harvest them after the tenancy ends.
Government's power to take private property for public use with just compensation, through condemnation.
The broker who runs a brokerage firm, employs or engages other brokers, and is responsible for supervising them and the firm's trust accounts.
An improvement that extends onto a neighbor's property or into a setback or easement.
Any claim or right held by someone other than the owner that limits the property's use or lowers its value, such as a lien, easement, or restriction.

Federal law barring credit discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, marital status, age, receipt of public-assistance income, or good-faith exercise of consumer credit rights.
A buyer's interest in property under a signed purchase contract before legal title passes at closing.
The owner's interest in a property: market value minus all loan balances.

Under the Colorado Foreclosure Protection Act, a buyer of a residence in foreclosure who won't occupy it as a principal residence. These sales carry special contract protections and cancellation rights.
Professional liability insurance required of every Active Colorado broker; minimum $100,000 per claim and $300,000 aggregate.
Transfer of property to the state when an owner dies without a will and without heirs.
A leasehold with a definite start and end date that ends automatically without notice.
A federal tax on the right to transfer property at death, based on the fair market value of the estate; most estates fall below the filing threshold.

A Commission addendum that lets either party structure the sale as a Section 1031 exchange. The other party cooperates at no added cost, and the contract binds both parties even if the exchange fails.
A listing with one broker in which the owner keeps the right to sell the property alone without owing a commission.
A listing in which the broker earns a commission no matter who sells the property during the term, including the owner.
The Commission's landlord-side listing contract. It hires a brokerage to market a property for lease and find a tenant.
aliases: Exclusive Right to Lease Listing Contract

glossary.definition: A listing in which the brokerage earns its fee if the property sells during the listing period, no matter who finds the buyer.
A contract that all parties have fully performed.
A contract with obligations still to be performed.
A small household or domestic well permitted by the State Engineer outside the priority system, with limited uses.
Agency created by words, oral or written, such as a signed listing agreement.
A contract whose terms are stated in words, oral or written.
Coverage, often called tail coverage, that lets claims be reported after an E&O policy ends; Colorado requires a 365-day option.
Loss in value from conditions outside the property, such as noise or a declining local economy; always incurable.
Title VIII of the Civil Rights Act of 1968, as amended, which prohibits housing discrimination based on seven protected classes.
Having one or more children under 18 living with a parent, custodian or designee; includes pregnancy and someone securing custody.
A general lien the IRS holds on all of a taxpayer's property after an assessed tax goes unpaid; a public notice is filed to establish priority against most creditors.
The most complete form of ownership, unlimited in duration and freely transferable or inheritable.
A fee estate that can end if a stated condition occurs or stops, such as a fee simple determinable or a fee simple subject to a condition subsequent.
A loan insured by the Federal Housing Administration and made by an approved lender, known for low down payments.
A person in a position of trust who must act in the best interests of the client.
Federal law requiring withholding at closing when the seller is a foreign person.
aliases: Foreign Investment in Real Property Tax Act

glossary.definition: The Financial Institutions Reform, Recovery, and Enforcement Act of 1989, whose Title XI created the federal framework for appraiser standards and state appraiser licensing.
Formerly personal property that has been attached to real estate so that it becomes part of the real property.
The legal process by which a lender forces the sale of property to satisfy a defaulted loan.
Person who, for pay, offers to stop or delay a foreclosure or arrange relief for a homeowner; regulated by the CFPA.
Intentional misstatement or concealment of a material fact to induce someone to act, causing them harm.
An ownership interest of indefinite duration, such as a fee simple or life estate.
Loss in value from poor design or outdated features within the property; may be curable or incurable.
An agent authorized to handle a range of matters in a particular business, such as a property manager.
A deed in which the grantor warrants title against all defects, including those arising before the grantor owned the property.
Funds received and available for immediate withdrawal, such as wires or cashier's checks, required before a Colorado closing provider disburses.
The intangible value of a business's reputation, name and customer relationships.
A lease with rent that increases in scheduled steps.
The person who receives title by deed.
The person who conveys title by deed.
Sales price divided by annual gross income; used for larger or commercial income property.
A lease where the tenant pays fixed rent and the landlord pays property expenses.
Sales price divided by monthly gross rent; used to estimate value of 1–4 unit rentals.
A long-term lease of land only, on which the tenant usually builds.
Competitors agreeing not to do business with a particular person or firm.
The implied warranty in most states that residential rental premises are fit to live in.
Describes an oil and gas lease that continues past its primary term because production in paying quantities continues.
Home equity line of credit: a revolving credit line secured by the borrower's home.
The closer supervision an employing broker must give new brokers: training, contract help, transaction monitoring, and closing review.
The legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible use that produces the highest value.
The Division of Real Estate office that registers HOAs, educates owners and logs complaints. It is not a regulator and has no enforcement power.
A listing provision that protects the commission for a period after expiration, limited to buyers whose names were given to the seller in writing during the term.
A period after a listing or buyer agreement ends during which the broker can still earn compensation from prospects named in writing during the term.
Federal rule (Section 121) letting a seller exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 married filing jointly) on a main home owned and used at least 2 of the last 5 years.
An organization of owners in a planned community or condominium that enforces CC&Rs, maintains common areas, and collects assessments.
Internet Data Exchange: the MLS feature that lets participants display other participants' listings on their websites under MLS rules.
Agency created by the conduct of the parties rather than by an express agreement.
A contract created by the parties' conduct rather than stated words.
A drawing by a surveyor showing where improvements sit relative to the boundaries. It is less precise than a full survey.
Knowledge legally treated as known by someone else. In Colorado, a designated single agent's knowledge is not imputed to non-designated brokers in the firm.
A license that remains renewed but can't be used for brokerage activity; no E&O required while inactive.
A broker who runs their own one-person brokerage and doesn't employ or supervise other brokers; requires two years of Active licensure.
A worker who controls how the work is done and pays their own self-employment taxes, as opposed to an employee.
The published market rate an adjustable-rate loan is tied to; it changes over time.
A lease whose rent adjusts with an economic index, such as the Consumer Price Index.
Permission given after the person understands what will be disclosed or done and its consequences.
The buyer's written notice listing unsatisfactory conditions and the corrections requested, delivered by the Inspection Objection Deadline.
The Commission form, signed by buyer and seller, in which the seller agrees to specific corrections. It amends the contract.
A sale in which the seller receives at least one payment after the tax year of the sale, usually reporting gain as payments are received.
A court action in which a holder of disputed money deposits it with the court and asks the court to decide who gets it.
Dying without a valid will. Property then passes to heirs under state succession laws.
A lawsuit by an owner seeking compensation when government action has effectively taken or damaged the property without formal condemnation.
Transfer of title without the owner's consent, such as by foreclosure, eminent domain, escheat, or adverse possession.
Co-ownership with equal shares and the right of survivorship, traditionally requiring the four unities of possession, interest, time, and title.
A trust account's chronological record of every receipt and disbursement, with a running balance.
A conventional loan that exceeds the conforming loan limit set for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.
A sale in which the seller keeps legal title until the buyer pays in full; the buyer has possession and equitable title.
A hidden defect not discoverable by ordinary inspection.
The federally required disclosure for housing built before 1978, including known hazards, the EPA pamphlet and the buyer's inspection opportunity.
A lease that gives the tenant the right, but not the obligation, to buy the property.
A tenant's right to possess property for a period under a lease. It's treated as personal property.
A trust account record kept separately for each beneficiary, showing that person's receipts, disbursements and balance.
An informal reprimand sent by certified mail for minor misconduct; the licensee can reject it by requesting formal proceedings within 20 days.
A preliminary document summarizing proposed deal terms, usually non-binding on the main transaction.
Personal, revocable permission to enter another's land for a specific purpose. It isn't an interest in land.
A Commission addendum for a purchase contract in which a licensee buys the seller's property. The seller may terminate at any time and reimburses the licensee's expenses up to a stated cap.
A creditor's claim against property as security for a debt, which can be enforced by forcing a sale.
The view, followed in most states, that a mortgage creates only a lien and the borrower keeps title; contrasts with title theory.
An estate that lasts for the lifetime of a named person, after which the property passes to a remainderman or reverts to the grantor.
A Section 1031 trade of real property held for investment or business use for other such property, deferring tax on the gain.
Colorado's term for a single agent whose duties are only those set by statute plus any additional duties agreed in writing.
An amount agreed in advance as the remedy for breach. In the Colorado contract, it is the earnest money kept by the seller as the seller's only remedy unless specific performance is selected.
A buyer taking over the seller's existing loan; the balance is debited to the seller and credited to the buyer.
TRID form the lender must deliver or mail within three business days after receiving a loan application.
The loan amount divided by the lesser of the sales price or appraised value.
A legal description that identifies a parcel by lot and block number on a recorded subdivision plat.
A rental agreement for the space a manufactured home sits on, usually in a park. A buyer of the home must be approved by the lot owner and take over the lease or sign a new one.
The written contract between an owner and a property manager that creates the agency and sets duties and compensation.
The fixed percentage a lender adds to the index to set an ARM's rate.
Competitors dividing markets by territory, customers or property type.
The price actually paid for a property in a specific sale; it may differ from market value.
The most probable price a property should bring in a competitive, open market with typically motivated, informed parties and reasonable exposure time.
Title free enough from reasonable doubt that a prudent buyer would accept it.
A fact that would affect a reasonable person's decision to buy or the price they'd pay.
Mutual execution of contract: the date both parties have signed the contract. Many deadlines are counted from it.
A specific, involuntary lien for unpaid contractors, subcontractors, or suppliers who improved the property.
A nonbinding process in which a neutral third party helps the parties settle. Colorado contracts require it before arbitration or litigation.
A legal description that traces a parcel's boundaries using distances, directions, and monuments from a point of beginning back to that point.
Property tax rate expressed in mills (thousandths of a dollar) per dollar of assessed value.
Ownership of minerals beneath the surface, which can be severed from surface ownership.
The Commission's position that every broker must perform all statutory duties of a single agent or transaction-broker; those duties can't be waived.
Routine help a broker may give a customer, such as showing property, filling in forms, or conveying offers, without creating a brokerage relationship.
A false statement of material fact that the other party relies on; it may be innocent, negligent or intentional.
Funds a broker holds that are not the broker's own, such as earnest money, rents, security deposits and advance payments.
A two-party security instrument in which the borrower (mortgagor) pledges property to the lender (mortgagee) as collateral.
A separately licensed person who takes residential loan applications or negotiates residential loan terms; brokers without this license shouldn't negotiate seller-financing loan terms.
A private organization through which member brokers share listing information to cooperate in finding buyers.
An increase in loan balance when payments are too small to cover the interest due.
A lease where the tenant pays rent plus some or all of the property's expenses.
A listing in which the seller names a net price and the broker keeps anything above it; not expressly prohibited in Colorado but discouraged, with no Commission-approved form.
Effective gross income minus operating expenses; excludes debt service and income tax depreciation.
The deadline by which the buyer may terminate if the lender's underwriting is unsatisfactory. Missing it can make the earnest money nonrefundable.
A use that was lawful before a zoning change but doesn't meet the current ordinance. It may continue, usually with limits.
Document recorded by the public trustee that starts a Colorado foreclosure.
The written notice a party delivers to end the contract under a specific provision. It is effective when the other party receives it by the deadline.
Replacing a contract or party with a new one by agreement, releasing the original party.
Matters affecting title that don't appear in the public records, such as unrecorded easements, boundary disputes or parties in possession.
A proposal showing willingness to be bound on definite terms, which becomes a contract when accepted.
The written policies every employing broker must adopt and have each associate receive and sign, including brokerage relationships and confidentiality.
A lease in which a mineral owner (lessor) grants an oil company (lessee) the right to explore for and produce oil and gas in exchange for a bonus, rentals and royalties.
Memory aid for the six fiduciary duties: obedience, loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, reasonable care and diligence.
A nonexclusive listing given to one or more brokers; only the broker who is the procuring cause earns a fee.
A projection of a property's income and expenses for a year.
A contract giving the optionee the right, but not the obligation, to buy property at a set price within a set time, for consideration.
Optional title coverage that removes the standard exceptions for unrecorded matters such as parties in possession, survey issues and unrecorded mechanics' liens.
Title policy protecting the buyer's ownership; under the Colorado contract default, the seller pays for it.
Paid after the period it covers; Colorado property taxes are paid the year after they're levied.
The amount needed to pay a loan in full at closing, including accrued interest; a seller debit when the seller's loan is retired.
A lease with base rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales, common in retail.
A leasehold that renews automatically for successive periods, such as month to month, until notice is given.
Movable property that isn't real property, such as furniture or vehicles. It transfers by bill of sale.
A fiduciary deed used by the court-appointed representative of a deceased person's estate to convey estate property.
A study of a property's history and records to identify possible contamination, used to support CERCLA defenses.
Principal, interest, taxes and insurance — the components of a typical monthly mortgage payment.
The fixed starting point of a metes and bounds description, where the description must also end.
Government's authority to regulate property use to protect public health, safety, and welfare. It's the basis of zoning and building codes.
Commission guidance (CP-1, CP-2, etc.) explaining how it views practice issues; best practices, not binding law.
A Commission optional form for a seller rent-back: the seller stays in the home after closing for a short term of no more than 60 days.
A written document authorizing one person (the attorney-in-fact) to act for another.
An easement acquired by open, continuous, hostile use of another's land for the period set by state law.
Scheduled upkeep designed to prevent problems and preserve value.
Competitors agreeing on prices or commission rates.
The initial period of an oil and gas lease during which the lessee must begin drilling or production.
A party to a transaction acting for themselves, such as a broker buying or selling their own property.
Colorado's water doctrine: the first person to put water to beneficial use has the senior right.
aliases: first in time, first in right

glossary.definition: Insurance protecting a conventional lender against borrower default, typically required with a small down payment.
A disciplinary order letting a licensee keep practicing subject to conditions set by the Commission.
The borrower's written promise to repay a debt on stated terms. In seller financing, it is secured by a deed of trust.
A licensee or firm hired as a general agent to operate income property for an owner.
Dividing an expense or income between buyer and seller according to the time each owned the property.
A group protected from discrimination by law; federally: race, color, religion, national origin, sex, disability and familial status.
Property associated with facts like a homicide, other felony or suicide, or an occupant's disease highly unlikely to spread by occupancy. Not material facts under C.R.S. 38-35.5-101.
The county official who serves as trustee under Colorado deeds of trust and conducts foreclosures and releases.
Exaggerated opinion or sales talk that a reasonable person would not rely on as fact.
An independent party who holds sale proceeds during a 1031 exchange so the investor never has control of the cash.
Federal tax category for a licensed agent paid on output under a written non-employee contract; not treated as an employee for federal employment taxes.
A tenant's or owner's right to possess and use property without interference from the landlord or someone with superior title.
A lawsuit to establish ownership and remove clouds on title.
A deed that conveys whatever interest the grantor has, if any, with no warranties.
Recording system where a later buyer without notice of an earlier unrecorded interest wins by recording first; Colorado's system.
A naturally occurring, odorless radioactive gas from uranium decay in soil; EPA action level is 4 pCi/L.
A principal's approval, after the fact, of an act an agent performed without authority, creating agency for that act.
The Commission's term for a broker's licensed or unlicensed assistant; unlicensed REAPs may do clerical work but not negotiate or advise.
A state fund some states keep to pay consumers who can't collect judgments against licensees. Colorado repealed its fund in 2005 and has none today.
Land, everything permanently attached to it, and the legal rights of ownership.
Form TD-1000 filed with a deed to report the sale price to the county assessor; confidential.
A change in rules, policies, practices or services that gives a person with a disability equal opportunity to use housing.
A physical change to the premises that a person with a disability needs; generally at the tenant's expense in private housing.
Returning part of the firm's earned commission to its own client; allowed in Colorado with proper written and lender disclosure.
A bank, savings and loan or credit union insured by the FDIC or NCUA. For Colorado trust accounts it must be in Colorado.
Title as shown in the public records and the title commitment, including recorded liens, easements and covenants.
Filing a document affecting real property in the county public records, which gives constructive notice.
A grid-based legal description system using principal meridians, base lines, townships, and sections. It's used in most western and midwestern states.
Buying back property after a foreclosure sale; in Colorado available to junior lienors, not the owner.
Illegally refusing to lend, or lending on worse terms, in an area because of its racial or ethnic makeup.
Compensation for referring a client; allowed between licensees with reasonable cause and if RESPA permits, but never to unlicensed persons.
Principle that a superior property loses value when surrounded by lesser properties; its opposite is progression.
Provision in a blanket loan that frees individual parcels from the lien as they are paid down.
Canceling a contract and returning the parties to their original positions.
Under the CFPA, an owner's principal residence with a home loan at least 30 days delinquent or in default.
A Commission addendum attached to the Commercial or Land contract when the property includes dwellings. It brings in residential disclosures such as lead-based paint and carbon monoxide alarms.
Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act; requires settlement-cost disclosures and bans kickbacks and unearned fees for settlement services.
A loan for older homeowners in which the lender pays the owner and the balance grows, repaid when the owner sells, moves or dies.
The right to match a third-party offer before the owner sells to that third party.
The feature of joint tenancy under which a deceased owner's interest passes automatically to the surviving co-owners.
Rights of owners of land along a river or stream to make reasonable use of the water.
Managing exposure to loss by avoiding, controlling, transferring or retaining risk.
The mineral owner's fractional share of oil or gas production, paid free of production costs.
Day-to-day rules adopted by an association's board, such as parking, pets and amenities. They must be consistent with the declaration.
The market where existing loans are bought, sold and securitized by entities such as Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae.
In the rectangular survey system, a 1-mile-square area containing 640 acres. There are 36 in a township.
A tax-deferred like-kind exchange of investment or business real estate under Internal Revenue Code Section 1031.
Money a tenant pays to secure performance of a lease; in Colorado capped at two months' rent and returned within one month (up to 60 days by lease).
Seller financing in which the seller accepts the buyer's note for part of the price; debited to the seller and credited to the buyer.
A single agent who represents only the seller (listing agent). In leasing, the landlord's agent plays the same role.
The Commission form a seller completes from current actual knowledge about the property's condition. It is not a warranty.
A working spreadsheet used to compute closing figures, with debit and credit columns for the seller, the buyer and the broker's cash; Colorado courses teach a six-column version.
Ownership by a single person or legal entity.
Sale where the lender agrees to accept less than the loan balance and release its lien.
Negotiating a listing directly with an owner who has an unexpired exclusive listing with another firm; prohibited.
A broker engaged by and representing only one party in a transaction: a seller's, buyer's, landlord's or tenant's agent.
A closing item between one party and an outside payee or source, entered in that party's column and the cash column.
Colorado protected class covering lawful, verifiable income, including rental assistance and vouchers.
The Commission addendum in which the seller identifies the property's water source: a well (with permit number), a water provider, or another source.
An agent authorized for one specific act or transaction, such as a listing broker.
A one-time association charge for a specific expense, such as a major repair, on top of regular dues.
FEMA-mapped area with a 1% annual chance of flooding (Zones A and V); flood insurance required with federally backed loans.
Local government unit, such as a metropolitan district, that can issue debt and levy property taxes for services or infrastructure.
A deed in which the grantor warrants title only against defects arising during the grantor's ownership.
A court order requiring a party to carry out the contract, for example to convey the property.
The Commission form, completed by the listing licensee, stating how square footage was measured or sourced. It is for marketing only.
A statement from the owners' association showing the owner's account status and fees, requested by the seller before closing.
Law requiring certain contracts, including contracts to sell real estate, to be in writing and signed to be enforceable.
The deadline set by state law for filing a lawsuit; after it passes, the claim can't be enforced.
Directing buyers or renters toward or away from areas based on a protected class.
Property that buyers may avoid for psychological reasons, such as a death or crime there, rather than physical defects.
A negotiated settlement of a disciplinary case between the licensee and the Commission; it becomes a public record.
A broker engaged to act for another broker on a principal's behalf. Colorado single agents and transaction-brokers may not create subagents.
A tenant's transfer of part of its leasehold interest; the original tenant remains liable and acts as the subtenant's landlord.
Under the listing contract, a person the broker negotiated with whose name was given to the seller in writing during the listing period.
An agreement by which a lien holder accepts a lower priority than another lien.
Principle that a buyer won't pay more for a property than the cost of an equally desirable alternative.
Colorado's limited priority for an HOA's assessment lien over a first deed of trust, for up to six months of regular common-expense assessments.
A broker, such as a managing broker or team lead, to whom the employing broker has delegated supervisory duties in writing.
The permanent, long-term loan that pays off the construction lender when the project is finished.
Telephone Consumer Protection Act; federal law restricting autodialed and prerecorded calls and texts.
Two or more brokers in the same brokerage firm who regularly work together; team names can't suggest a separate company.
Occupancy by a tenant who stays after the lease ends without the landlord's consent.
A leasehold of no fixed term that lasts as long as both parties wish.
A form of co-ownership for married couples, recognized in some states, with survivorship and protection from one spouse acting alone. Colorado does not recognize it.
Co-ownership with undivided interests that may be unequal, transferable without consent, and inheritable, with no right of survivorship.
Alterations made to leased space to suit a tenant's use, often funded partly by a landlord allowance.
A private nonprofit authorized by Congress under FIRREA that houses the boards setting appraisal standards (USPAP) and appraiser qualifications; it does not license appraisers.
Money or tangible non-monetary assets exchanged in a transaction; must be itemized in contracts and can't be paid as illegal referral kickbacks.
A monthly check that the journal balance, the total of all ledgers, and the reconciled bank balance agree on the same date.
Conditioning the sale of one product or service on the purchase of another.
A contract clause making deadlines strict. A late performance or notice is a breach or is ineffective.

An optional time in the Dates and Deadlines table that sets the cutoff for objection, resolution, examination and termination deadlines. If blank or N/A, those deadlines end at 11:59 p.m. Mountain Time.
Ownership or use of property divided by recurring time periods, either as a fee interest (timeshare estate) or a contractual right to use.
A policy that protects an owner or lender against covered losses from title defects. It's paid for with a one-time premium.
In the rectangular survey system, a square 6 miles on a side (36 square miles) divided into 36 sections.
Equipment a tenant installs for business use. It remains the tenant's personal property and must be removed by the end of the lease.
A business name other than the firm's legal name, filed with the Commission; a firm may use only one.
A licensee who assists one or both parties in a transaction without acting as an advocate for either; duties are set by state law.
The documents a broker must keep for each transaction, per the Commission's checklist, for four years.
A broker who helps one or more parties through a transaction without being an agent or advocate for any of them. Colorado's presumed relationship absent a written agency agreement.
TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure rule, which created the Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure.
Specific credit terms in an advertisement (down payment, number of payments, payment amount, finance charge) that require full TILA disclosures.
A net lease where the tenant pays rent plus property taxes, insurance and maintenance.
An arrangement in which a trustor conveys property to a trustee, who holds legal title and manages it for a beneficiary.
A separate fiduciary account at a recognized depository that holds money belonging to others. Colorado rules call it a trust or escrow account.
Federal law, implemented by Regulation Z, requiring disclosure of credit costs including the APR.
A monthly check that the journal balance matches the reconciled bank balance; used for a broker's own non-brokerage trust account.
The Uniform Electronic Transactions Act, a state law adopted by nearly all states that validates electronic records and signatures.
Giving legal advice or drafting legal documents without a law license, such as advising on title exceptions or writing custom contract clauses.
A buried tank holding fuel or chemicals that can leak and contaminate soil and groundwater.
The lender's process of evaluating a borrower's capacity, credit, capital and collateral to decide whether to make a loan.
Using a position of trust or control to obtain someone's agreement unfairly; makes a contract voidable.
A contract in which one party promises something in exchange for an act; only that party is bound.
An agent with broad authority to do anything the principal could legally delegate.
Insulation used in the 1970s that can release formaldehyde gas.
Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice — the generally accepted ethical and performance standards for appraisers in the U.S.
aliases: Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice

glossary.definition: A loan to an eligible veteran or service member that is partly guaranteed by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Permission to depart from the strict requirements of a zoning ordinance because they would cause an unusual hardship.
Legal responsibility for someone else's acts. Colorado clients are not vicariously liable for broker acts they did not approve, direct or ratify.
An agreement with no legal effect, such as one for an illegal purpose.
A contract that is valid until the protected party chooses to cancel it, such as one signed by a minor.
Implied promise in every Colorado residential lease that the unit is fit for human habitation; cannot be waived.
A property right to divert and use a certain amount of water, which in Colorado can be conveyed separately from land.
Land saturated with water much of the time, protected under the Clean Water Act.
In real estate, the theft of closing funds by tricking a party into wiring money to a criminal's account, usually with fake wiring instructions.
A new loan that includes an existing loan, with the wrap lender continuing to pay the underlying loan.
Local laws dividing land into districts and regulating the uses, density, and building dimensions allowed in each.

references.title: The exam at a glance
references.body:
The Colorado broker exam is given by PSI in two portions. Each is scored separately, and you must pass both. Source: PSI's Colorado candidate bulletin; check the current bulletin before you schedule.

| | National portion | State portion |
|---|---|---|
| Scored questions | 80 | 74 |
| Time | 120 minutes | 110 minutes |
| To pass | 60 correct (75%) | 53 correct (about 72%) |

- PSI may add a handful of unscored pretest questions. You can't tell which ones they are, so answer everything.
- You can pass the portions on different days. A passing score on a portion is good for one year, and you have one year after passing to apply for your license.
- No reference materials are allowed in the room, and personal calculators are on PSI's prohibited list. You get scratch paper.

## National portion: where the points are

| Area | Weight | About this many questions |
|---|---|---|
| Contracts | 19% | 15 |
| Agency | 13% | 10 |
| Practice of real estate (fair housing, antitrust, advertising, supervision) | 12% | 10 |
| Property ownership | 10% | 8 |
| Financing | 9% | 7 |
| Valuation | 8% | 6 |
| Property disclosures | 7% | 6 |
| Transfer of title | 6% | 5 |
| Real estate calculations | 6% | 5 |
| Land use controls | 5% | 4 |
| Property management | 5% | 4 |

## State portion: where the points are

| Area | Questions (of 74) |
|---|---|
| Colorado forms and contracts | 23 |
| Activities of licensees | 11 |
| Brokerage relationships | 11 |
| Closing and settlement | 10 |
| Additional topics: property management and landlord-tenant, water rights and wells, Colorado taxes, Colorado Fair Housing Act, foreclosure | 7 |
| Licensing requirements | 5 |
| Record keeping and trust accounts | 5 |
| Commission duties and powers | 2 |

> **Strategy:** Contracts are the largest area on both portions. Colorado forms alone are almost a third of the state exam, so know the residential Contract to Buy and Sell well: who does what, by which deadline, and what happens if they don't.

## How this course's practice exams work

Each timed practice exam draws 80 national and 74 state questions at random from the 250-question bank and scores each portion against its own pass mark, like the real thing. The timer is the combined 230 minutes.

references.title: Math formulas
references.body:
## Core formulas

| To find | Formula |
|---|---|
| Commission | Sale price × commission rate |
| Seller's net | Sale price − commission − loan payoff − seller's other costs |
| Price needed to net a target | (Desired net + seller's costs) ÷ (1 − commission rate) |
| Loan amount | Price (or appraised value, if lower) × LTV |
| LTV | Loan ÷ value |
| Points | Loan amount × number of points × 1% |
| Annual interest (simple) | Principal × annual rate |
| Monthly interest | Principal × annual rate ÷ 12 |
| Equity | Market value − debts against the property |
| NOI | Gross potential income − vacancy and collection loss − operating expenses (not debt service) |
| Cap rate | NOI ÷ value |
| Value by income approach | NOI ÷ cap rate |
| Gross rent multiplier value | Monthly gross rent × GRM |
| Percent profit | (Sale price − cost) ÷ cost |
| Property tax | Assessed value × mill levy ÷ 1,000 |

## The "IRV" triangle

Income = Rate × Value. Cover the one you want: Value = Income ÷ Rate, Rate = Income ÷ Value. The same pattern works for commission (Commission = Rate × Price) and interest (Interest = Rate × Principal).

## Land

- 1 acre = 43,560 square feet
- 1 section = 1 square mile = 640 acres
- 1 township = 36 sections = 6 miles × 6 miles
- Rectangular survey shortcut: multiply 640 by each fraction in the description. For example, the NE ¼ of the SW ¼ is 640 × ¼ × ¼ = 40 acres.
- 1 mile = 5,280 feet; 1 square yard = 9 square feet

## Prorations

1. Find the amount per day (or per month).
2. Count the days the party is responsible for.
3. Multiply. Decide who gets the credit.

| Item | Typical direction |
|---|---|
| Colorado property taxes (paid in arrears) | The seller hasn't paid this year's taxes yet: **debit seller, credit buyer** for the seller's days |
| Rent the seller already collected for the month | **Debit seller, credit buyer** for the buyer's days |
| HOA dues the seller prepaid | **Credit seller, debit buyer** for the buyer's days |
| Security deposits held by the seller | **Debit seller, credit buyer** (the buyer takes over the obligation) |

- The Colorado residential contract prorates to the closing date. Unless the parties choose otherwise, taxes are based on the calendar year before closing, using the most recent mill levy and valuation.
- The exam question will tell you the day count convention (365-day year or 30-day "banker's" months) and who owns the closing day. Read for it.

## Colorado-specific numbers
